knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetry-Breaking Constraints Relative to a Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the source's existential conditions for symmetry-breaking constraints relative to a permutation or group action on a specified set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(\pi\in S_n\) act on vector components, and let \(g(x)\leq0\) abbreviate \(g_i(x)\leq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,q\). The inequalities are symmetry-breaking constraints with respect to \(\pi\) and \(X\) if there exists \(y\in X\) such that \(g(y\pi)\leq0\). For a group \(G\), they are symmetry-breaking constraints with respect to \(G\) and \(X\) if there exists \(y\in XG\) such that \(g(y)\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to X, the constraints are symmetry breaking for pi if some y in X has its permuted point y pi satisfy them. For a group G, they are symmetry breaking if some point in XG satisfies them.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathbb R^n
\pi\in S_n
g(x)\leq0\text{ abbreviates }g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,q
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{SBC}_{\pi,X}(g)\iff\exists y\in X:\ g(y\pi)\leq0,\qquad \operatorname{SBC}_{G,X}(g)\iff\exists y\in XG:\ g(y)\leq0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a formulation whose feasible set maps into that of the original problem, whose global solutions map to global solutions, and whose infeasibility implies infeasibility of the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a problem \(P\), a formulation \(Q\) is a narrowing of \(P\) if there exists \(\eta:\mathcal F(Q)\to\mathcal F(P)\) such that \(\eta(\mathcal G(Q))\subseteq\mathcal G(P)\), and if \(Q\) is infeasible only if \(P\) is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Q is a narrowing of P when a map sends every feasible point of Q into the feasible set of P and sends global solutions of Q to global solutions of P, while Q being infeasible implies that P is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is a problem}
Q\text{ is a formulation of the prescribed form}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A binary vertex-pairing formulation that maximizes the number of preserved edge pairings between two ordered graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G_1=(V_1,E_1)$ and $G_2=(V_2,E_2)$ have ordered vertex sets, and let $Q=\{(i,j,k,l):(i,k)\in E_1,(j,l)\in E_2\}$. Introduce $x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ to indicate that $i\in V_1$ is paired with $j\in V_2$, and variables $w_{ijkl}$ indicating paired edges. The order-preserving matching model is
\[
\max \sum_{(i,j,k,l)\in Q}w_{ijkl}
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{i\in V_1}x_{ij}\le 1\quad(\forall j\in V_2),\qquad
\sum_{j\in V_2}x_{ij}\le 1\quad(\forall i\in V_1),
\]
\[
w_{ijkl}\le x_{ij},\qquad w_{ijkl}\le x_{kl}\quad(\forall(i,j,k,l)\in Q),
\]
and
\[
x_{ij}+x_{kl}\le1\quad\text{whenever }i<k\text{ and }l<j.
\]
The first two constraint families make the vertex pairing injective in both directions, the linking constraints permit an edge pairing only when its endpoints are correspondingly paired, and the final family excludes crossings. Because every $w_{ijkl}$ has positive objective coefficient and binary upper bounds, an optimal solution exists with $w_{ijkl}\in\{0,1\}$ even when the $w$ variables are declared free continuous variables; explicit integrality and nonnegativity restrictions on them are therefore unnecessary for optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Match vertices of two ordered graphs injectively, link each candidate edge match to its two endpoint matches, and forbid reversed-order pairs. Maximizing the sum of edge-match variables then maximizes the number of preserved paired edges. The edge-match variables may be free and continuous because, at an optimum, their binary upper bounds and positive objective coefficients give them binary, nonnegative values.
assumptions_latex: G_1=(V_1,E_1)\text{ and }G_2=(V_2,E_2)\text{ have ordered vertex sets}
x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\quad(\forall i\in V_1,\,j\in V_2)
\text{Each }w_{ijkl}\text{ occurs in the maximization objective with positive coefficient and satisfies }w_{ijkl}\le x_{ij},\ w_{ijkl}\le x_{kl}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The formulation yields an injective, noncrossing vertex pairing maximizing paired edges, and it has an optimum with }w_{ijkl}\in\{0,1\}\text{ without explicitly imposing }w_{ijkl}\ge0\text{ or integrality.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orbits and setwise stabilizers of a permutation group
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation-group structures used by orbit- and stabilizer-based symmetry methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a permutation group \(G\le\Sigma_n\), the orbit of \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is \[\operatorname{orb}_G(i)=\{\pi(i):\pi\in G\}.\] Orbit membership is symmetric, and the distinct orbits partition \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the setwise stabilizer is \[\operatorname{stabil}(S,G)=\{\pi\in G:\pi(S)=S\},\] and it is a subgroup of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The orbit of an index is the set of indices reachable from it under the permutation group. The distinct orbits partition the index set. The setwise stabilizer of a subset consists of the group elements mapping that subset onto itself, and it is a subgroup.
assumptions_latex: G\le\Sigma_n
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\operatorname{orb}_G(i):i=1,\ldots,n\}\text{ induces a partition of }\{1,\ldots,n\},\qquad \operatorname{stabil}(S,G)\le G

source_evidence.locator: Enumeration / 9.3. Dealing with Symmetries / Definition 9.3-extra-5

knowledge_statements.title: Orbits and setwise stabilizers of a permutation group

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when the action induced on a subset respects group composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\leq S_n\), let \(\omega\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), set \(H=\operatorname{Sym}(\omega)\), and define \(\psi:G\to H\) by \(\psi(\pi)=\pi[\omega]\). Then \(\psi\) is a group homomorphism if and only if \(G\) stabilizes \(\omega\) setwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The induced action on omega is a group homomorphism exactly when every element of G maps omega onto itself.
assumptions_latex: G\leq S_n
\omega\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}
H=\operatorname{Sym}(\omega)
\psi(\pi)=\pi[\omega]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi\text{ is a group homomorphism}\iff (\forall\pi\in G)\;\pi(\omega)=\omega.

children.title: Optimization Symmetry Notions
children.top_down_role: Distinctions among symmetries of encodings, optimization problems, feasible solutions, and relaxations.

children.title: Formulation Symmetries
children.top_down_role: Symmetries visible in a selected algebraic or solver representation.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is an optimization formulation with represented decision space \(X\), feasible set \(F\subseteq X\), and objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\).
\(T:X\to X\) is a bijection expressible in the selected formulation or solver representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(F)=F\) and \(f(Tx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-dependent symmetry of an optimization formulation, including its objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a selected algebraic or solver representation of an optimization problem, with represented domain \(X\), feasible set \(F\), and objective \(f\). A bijection \(T:X\to X\) is a formulation symmetry of \(P\) when \(T(F)=F\) and \(f(Tx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). Thus \(T\) preserves feasibility and objective values in the represented variables. The resulting formulation-symmetry group is \(\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathrm{form}}(P)=\{T:T\text{ satisfies these conditions}\}\) under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formulation symmetry is a representation-visible bijection that maps feasible points to feasible points and preserves every feasible point's objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Formulation Symmetries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the formulation-symmetry container and is internally coherent, but no source is cited for the representation-dependent notion or the claimed group construction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Formulation symmetry group of a binary linear program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, invariance property, and formulation-dependence boundary for symmetries visible in a specified binary linear-programming formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\max\{c^\top x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\), with \(\pi(v)=(v_{\pi(1)},\ldots,v_{\pi(n)})\), define \[\Gamma=\{\pi\in\Sigma_n:\exists\sigma\in\Sigma_m\text{ such that }\pi(c)=c,\ \sigma(b)=b,\ A(\pi,\sigma)=A\}.\] Then \(\Gamma\) is a group. If \(\bar x\in[0,1]^n\) satisfies \(A\bar x\le b\) and \(\pi\in\Gamma\), then \(\pi(\bar x)\) is also relaxation-feasible and \(c^\top\pi(\bar x)=c^\top\bar x\). The vectors are called isomorphic solutions. The group is formulation-dependent and can change under positive constraint scaling or the addition or removal of redundant constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The formulation symmetry group consists of variable permutations that, together with a row permutation, preserve the objective vector, right-hand side, and constraint matrix. It is a group and maps each relaxation-feasible solution to an isomorphic solution with the same objective value. It depends on the chosen formulation, not solely on the relaxation's geometry.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\quad b\in\mathbb R^m,\quad c\in\mathbb R^n
\pi(v)=(v_{\pi(1)},\ldots,v_{\pi(n)})
A(\pi,\sigma)\text{ is obtained by the corresponding column and row permutations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma\le\Sigma_n,\qquad \bar x\in\{x\in[0,1]^n:Ax\le b\},\ \pi\in\Gamma\Rightarrow \pi(\bar x)\in\{x\in[0,1]^n:Ax\le b\},\ c^\top\pi(\bar x)=c^\top\bar x

children.title: Problem-Solution Symmetry Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Symmetries attached to the optimization problem or its solution space independently of a particular encoding.

children.title: Problem Symmetries
children.top_down_role: Transformations preserving the optimization problem independently of a particular encoding.

assumptions_latex: \(P=(X,F,f)\) is an optimization problem with feasible set \(F\subseteq X\).
\(g:X\to X\) is a bijection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(F)=F\) and \(f\circ g=f\) on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic feasible-set and objective invariance, independent of a particular constraint encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an optimization problem \(P=(X,F,f)\), a problem symmetry is a bijection \(g:X\to X\) satisfying \(g(F)=F\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for all \(x\in F\). The problem-symmetry set \(G_P=\{g:g(F)=F,\ f\circ g=f\text{ on }F\}\) is closed under composition and inversion and therefore forms a group. This definition concerns the optimization problem itself; an algebraic formulation may display only a subgroup of \(G_P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem symmetry bijectively preserves the feasible set and objective values, whether or not a chosen formulation makes that symmetry visible.
knowledge_statements.title: Problem Symmetries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intrinsic feasible-set and objective-invariance definition fits the leaf, but the record has no inspectable source supporting this precise notion or its distinction from formulation symmetry.

children.title: Solution-Space Symmetries
children.top_down_role: Transformations organizing feasible or optimal solutions into equivalent classes.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq X\) is a distinguished solution set, such as the set of all global minimizers.
\(h:S\to S\) is a bijection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\in\operatorname{Sym}(S)\), with composition as the group operation.

notation.meaning: permutation group of the solution set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Setwise symmetries of a specified solution set; additional structure may restrict admissible bijections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a distinguished solution set \(S\subseteq X\), for example \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\). A solution-space symmetry is a bijection \(h:S\to S\). If the solution space carries prescribed structure, such as adjacency, integrality classes, or distances, admissibility additionally requires \(h\) to preserve that structure. Under composition, all admissible solution-space symmetries form a subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sym}(S)\). This notion does not by itself require \(h\) to extend to a symmetry of the full feasible problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution-space symmetry permutes a specified set of solutions while preserving any structure declared part of that solution space.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Space Symmetries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition is coherent, but treating every structure-preserving bijection of a selected solution set as a solution-space symmetry requires a source specifying the intended solution-space structure and admissibility notion.

children.title: Problem-to-Solution Symmetry Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Alignment or divergence between problem invariance and symmetry visible in the solution space.

assumptions_latex: \(P=(X,F,f)\) has optimal solution set \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\).
\(g\) is a problem symmetry of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(S)=S\), and restriction defines a homomorphism \(\rho:G_P\to\operatorname{Sym}(S)\) by \(\rho(g)=g|_S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction of objective-preserving problem actions to the set of global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\) be nonempty, and let \(G_P\) be the group of problem symmetries of \(P=(X,F,f)\). For every \(g\in G_P\), feasibility and objective invariance imply \(g(S)=S\). Hence restriction induces a group homomorphism \(\rho:G_P\to\operatorname{Sym}(S)\), defined by \(\rho(g)=g|_S\). Its kernel consists of problem symmetries fixing every optimal solution. The map need not be surjective: a permutation of \(S\) may fail to extend to a feasibility- and objective-preserving bijection of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every problem symmetry permutes the global optima, but a symmetry of the optimal set need not extend to the entire problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Problem-to-Solution Symmetry Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restriction homomorphism and possible failure of surjectivity are mathematically sound and the property kind fits the correspondence leaf, but no source supports the stated correspondence.

children.title: Relaxation-Reformulation Symmetry Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Symmetries created, removed, or altered by relaxation, lifting, and reformulation.

children.title: Relaxation Symmetries
children.top_down_role: Symmetry introduced, removed, or enlarged after constraints or integrality requirements are relaxed.

assumptions_latex: \(R=(X_R,F_R,f_R)\) is a relaxation of an optimization model.
\(g:X_R\to X_R\) is a bijection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(F_R)=F_R\) and \(f_R(gx)=f_R(x)\) for every \(x\in F_R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry of the relaxed feasible region and relaxed objective, not necessarily of the original model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=(X_R,F_R,f_R)\) be a relaxation of an optimization model, so its feasible region contains the embedded original feasible set or otherwise yields the prescribed relaxation bound. A relaxation symmetry is a bijection \(g:X_R\to X_R\) satisfying \(g(F_R)=F_R\) and \(f_R(gx)=f_R(x)\) for every \(x\in F_R\). Relaxation symmetries form a group under composition. This group may strictly contain the symmetries induced by the original model because discarded constraints or integrality conditions can remove distinctions between variables or points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation symmetry preserves the relaxed feasible region and objective; relaxing constraints can create symmetries absent from the original model.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Symmetries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the relaxation-symmetry leaf, but the broad description of a relaxation and the claim that relaxation can create additional symmetries require authoritative support.

children.title: Reformulation Symmetries
children.top_down_role: Symmetry arising from alternative encodings, auxiliary variables, or lifted model structures.

assumptions_latex: \(Q=(Y,F_Q,f_Q)\) is a reformulation whose solutions map to an original problem through \(\pi:Y\to X\).
\(h:Y\to Y\) is a bijection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(F_Q)=F_Q\) and \(f_Q(hy)=f_Q(y)\) for every \(y\in F_Q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry of an extended or alternative formulation, including transformations of auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=(Y,F_Q,f_Q)\) reformulate an original problem, with a solution-preserving map \(\pi:Y\to X\). A reformulation symmetry is a bijection \(h:Y\to Y\) such that \(h(F_Q)=F_Q\) and \(f_Q(hy)=f_Q(y)\) for all \(y\in F_Q\). It is projection-trivial when \(\pi(hy)=\pi(y)\) for every \(y\in F_Q\); such a symmetry merely exchanges alternative lifted representations of the same original point. Other reformulation symmetries may project to genuine symmetries of the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reformulation symmetry preserves the reformulated model and may either permute original solutions or only exchange equivalent lifted representations.
knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation Symmetries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical definition and projection-trivial distinction fit the reformulation-symmetry container, but the precise reformulation and projection terminology is unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Symmetry Transfer Across Representations
children.top_down_role: Persistence or loss of symmetry when moving between equivalent model representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry Transfer Across Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivariant transfer through a surjective, objective-compatible representation map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Q=(Y,F_Q,f_Q)\) represents \(P=(X,F,f)\) through a surjection \(\pi:F_Q\to F\) satisfying \(f_Q=f\circ\pi\) on \(F_Q\). Let \(h:F_Q\to F_Q\) be a bijective symmetry of \(Q\). The symmetry \(h\) induces a bijection \(g:F\to F\) satisfying \(\pi\circ h=g\circ\pi\) exactly when \(h\) preserves fiber equivalence in both directions: for all \(y_1,y_2\in F_Q\), \(\pi(y_1)=\pi(y_2)\) if and only if \(\pi(hy_1)=\pi(hy_2)\). Under this condition, \(g(\pi(y))=\pi(hy)\) is well-defined and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetry of a representing formulation descends to a bijective symmetry of the original feasible problem exactly when it preserves projection-fiber equivalence in both directions.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=(Y,F_Q,f_Q)\) represents \(P=(X,F,f)\) through a surjection \(\pi:F_Q\to F\) satisfying \(f_Q=f\circ\pi\) on \(F_Q\).
\(h:F_Q\to F_Q\) is a bijective symmetry of \(Q\).
For all \(y_1,y_2\in F_Q\), \(\pi(y_1)=\pi(y_2)\) if and only if \(\pi(hy_1)=\pi(hy_2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rule \(g(\pi(y))=\pi(hy)\) defines a well-defined bijection \(g:F\to F\) satisfying \(\pi\circ h=g\circ\pi\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\).

children.title: Global Symmetry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Symmetries valid throughout the full model or search space.

assumptions_latex: \(P=(X,F,f)\) is an optimization problem.
\(G\) acts on all of \(X\) by bijections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(F)=F\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed symmetry group valid throughout the entire modeled decision space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A global symmetry regime for \(P=(X,F,f)\) is a group \(G\) acting on the entire decision space \(X\) such that every \(g\in G\) satisfies \(g(F)=F\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). The same action and invariance conditions apply without conditioning on a search node, partial assignment, face, or other local state. Consequently, each orbit \(Gx=\{gx:g\in G\}\) of a feasible point consists entirely of feasible points having the same objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a global regime, one fixed group preserves feasibility and objective values everywhere, without depending on a local search state or restricted region.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Symmetry Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally consistent and fits the global-regime leaf, but the specialized global-regime terminology and its contrast with local subsymmetry lack a source.

children.title: Local Subsymmetry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Symmetries activated only within restricted subproblems or search regions.

assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq X\) is a locally active domain, such as a face or branch-and-bound subproblem.
\(H_D\) acts bijectively on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(F\cap D)=F\cap D\) and \(f(hx)=f(x)\) for every \(h\in H_D\) and \(x\in F\cap D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry valid only after restricting the model to a specified local domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq X\) describe a local regime, such as a face induced by fixed variables or the domain of a branch-and-bound node. A local subsymmetry group \(H_D\) acts on \(D\) and satisfies \(h(F\cap D)=F\cap D\) and \(f(hx)=f(x)\) for every \(h\in H_D\) and \(x\in F\cap D\). Its elements need not extend to symmetries of \(F\) outside \(D\). Distinct local domains may therefore activate different groups, including transformations unavailable globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local subsymmetry preserves the restricted problem on a particular face or search subproblem but need not preserve the full model.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Subsymmetry Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restricted-domain invariance definition fits the local-subsymmetry leaf, but the precise subsymmetry notion and examples involving faces and branch-and-bound nodes require authoritative support.

children.title: Subsymmetry Activation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Search decisions or structural restrictions governing when local subsymmetries become available.

assumptions_latex: \(D(\alpha)\subseteq X\) is the domain determined by a local state \(\alpha\).
\(h:X\to X\) is a candidate transformation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is active at \(\alpha\) exactly when \(h(F\cap D(\alpha))=F\cap D(\alpha)\) and \(f(hx)=f(x)\) for all \(x\in F\cap D(\alpha)\).

notation.meaning: domain induced by the local state

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predicate delimiting local states on which a candidate transformation becomes a valid subsymmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha\) parameterize local states and let \(D(\alpha)\subseteq X\) be the corresponding restricted domain. For a candidate bijection \(h\), define its activation set by \(A_h=\{\alpha:h(F\cap D(\alpha))=F\cap D(\alpha),\ f(hx)=f(x)\text{ for all }x\in F\cap D(\alpha)\}\). The subsymmetry is active precisely for \(\alpha\in A_h\). A subsymmetry activation boundary is the boundary of \(A_h\) in the specified state space, or, for discrete states, the set of adjacent state transitions with exactly one endpoint in \(A_h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate subsymmetry activates exactly on local states where it preserves the restricted feasible set and objective; activation boundaries separate active and inactive states.
knowledge_statements.title: Subsymmetry Activation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The activation predicate is coherent, but the boundary notion depends on a specified topology or adjacency relation, and no source establishes this terminology or the intended state-space structure.

children.top_down_role: Action families distinguished by the transformed objects and admissible variable domains.

children.title: Variable-Permutation Actions
children.top_down_role: Actions permuting variables with compatible model roles.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\prod_{i=1}^n X_i\) is the decision domain.
\(\sigma\in S_n\) satisfies \(X_i=X_{\sigma(i)}\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((T_\sigma x)_i=x_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}\), and \(T_\sigma\) is a model symmetry exactly when it preserves feasibility and objective values.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate permutations restricted to variables with compatible domains and model roles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X=\prod_{i=1}^n X_i\) and a permutation \(\sigma\in S_n\) with compatible coordinate domains, define \(T_\sigma:X\to X\) by \((T_\sigma x)_i=x_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}\). A variable-permutation action is the group action \((\sigma,x)\mapsto T_\sigma x\). It is a symmetry action for \(P=(X,F,f)\) when \(T_\sigma(F)=F\) and \(f(T_\sigma x)=f(x)\) for every feasible \(x\) and every admitted \(\sigma\). Compatibility includes preservation of variable domains, integrality requirements, and all model roles affecting feasibility or cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable-permutation action reindexes compatible coordinates; it is symmetric when every admitted reindexing preserves the feasible set and objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Permutation Actions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinate action is correctly stated and fits the variable-permutation leaf, but no source supports the modeling compatibility conditions or the exact optimization-symmetry definition.

children.title: Signed-Permutation-Reflection Action Coupling
children.top_down_role: Actions combining coordinate permutations with domain-compatible reflections.

children.title: Signed-Permutation Actions
children.top_down_role: Coordinate permutations carrying domain-compatible sign changes.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is invariant under the proposed signed coordinate maps.
\(\sigma\in S_n\) and \(\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((T_{\varepsilon,\sigma}x)_i=\varepsilon_i x_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}\), with symmetry requiring \(T_{\varepsilon,\sigma}(F)=F\) and \(f\circ T_{\varepsilon,\sigma}=f\) on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear signed permutations about the origin; affine reflections about other centers require recentering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\sigma\in S_n\) and \(\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^n\), the signed-permutation map is \(T_{\varepsilon,\sigma}:X\to X\) defined by \((T_{\varepsilon,\sigma}x)_i=\varepsilon_i x_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}\). Admissibility requires this map to preserve the coordinate domains and variable types. It is a signed-permutation symmetry of \(P=(X,F,f)\) when \(T_{\varepsilon,\sigma}(F)=F\) and \(f(T_{\varepsilon,\sigma}x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). Admissible signed permutations form a subgroup of the signed symmetric group under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A signed-permutation action combines coordinate reindexing with sign changes and is symmetric when it preserves domains, feasibility, and objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Signed-Permutation Actions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The origin-centered signed-permutation formula is coherent and the definition kind fits the leaf, but the signed symmetric-group convention and exclusion of affine reflections require a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Reflection Actions
children.top_down_role: Domain-preserving reflections of individual coordinates or structured coordinate sets.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the feasible set of an optimization model with objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\).
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and the affine map \(r_c(x)=c-x\) preserves the variable domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_c\) is a reflection symmetry precisely when \(r_c(X)=X\) and \(f(r_c(x))=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Center vector determining the coordinatewise reflection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine coordinate reflection preserving feasibility and objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the feasible set and let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be the objective. For a vector \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define the affine reflection by \(r_c(x)=c-x\). The map \(r_c\) is a reflection action on the model if \(r_c(X)=X\); it is a reflection symmetry if additionally \(f(r_c(x))=f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\). Since \(r_c(r_c(x))=x\), the action is involutive. For binary variables, the coordinate reflection with \(c_i=1\) is complementation, \(x_i\mapsto 1-x_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reflection action is an involutive affine map that preserves the feasible set; it is a model symmetry when it also preserves every objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Reflection Actions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Reflection Actions leaf and is mathematically coherent, but no inspectable source is cited for the optimization-symmetry formulation or the binary-complementation specialization.

children.title: Permutation-Reflection Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Domain conditions governing compositions of coordinate permutations with reflections.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) define the optimization model.
\(P\) is a permutation matrix and \(r_c(x)=c-x\) is a domain-preserving reflection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The actions are compatible exactly when \(Pc=c\); under this condition \(P r_c=r_c P\), and all products \(P^k r_c^\varepsilon\) act consistently on the model when both generators preserve \(X\) and \(f\).

notation.meaning: Affine reflection determined by the center vector.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Commutation criterion for coordinate permutations and affine reflections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a permutation matrix and let \(r_c(x)=c-x\). Their actions are permutation-reflection compatible when they commute on the ambient variable domain. Directly, \(P r_c(x)=Pc-Px\) and \(r_c P(x)=c-Px\), so compatibility is equivalent to \(Pc=c\). If, in addition, \(P(X)=X\), \(r_c(X)=X\), \(f(Px)=f(x)\), and \(f(r_c(x))=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), then every composition generated by \(P\) and \(r_c\) is a symmetry of the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate permutation commutes with a reflection exactly when it fixes the reflection center; compatible symmetry generators then produce symmetry-preserving compositions.
knowledge_statements.title: Permutation-Reflection Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The commutation calculation and content kind fit the compatibility leaf, but the record has no cited source supporting this precise permutation-reflection criterion in the model-symmetry setting.

children.title: Value-Object Relabeling Action Family
children.top_down_role: Actions relabeling interchangeable values, classes, colors, or modeled objects.

children.title: Value-Relabeling Actions
children.top_down_role: Actions permuting interchangeable values within admissible variable domains.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite value set and \(x\in V^n\).
\(X\subseteq V^n\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) define the optimization model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A permutation \(\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(V)\) is a value-relabeling symmetry exactly when \(\sigma\cdot X=X\) and \(f(\sigma\cdot x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Finite set of admissible labels or values.
Permutation group of the value set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global relabeling of values used by discrete variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite value set and let \(\operatorname{Sym}(V)\) denote its permutation group. For \(\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(V)\) and \(x\in V^n\), define \((\sigma\cdot x)_i=\sigma(x_i)\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). This is a value-relabeling action. For a feasible set \(X\subseteq V^n\) and objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), the relabeling is a model symmetry when \(\sigma\cdot X=X\) and \(f(\sigma\cdot x)=f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value-relabeling action applies one permutation of the discrete value set to every variable value and is symmetric when feasibility and objective values are preserved.
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Relabeling Actions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The componentwise action is precise and fits Value-Relabeling Actions, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Object-Label Actions
children.top_down_role: Actions permuting labels attached to interchangeable classes, colors, or modeled objects.

assumptions_latex: \(O\) is a finite object set and \(x=(x_o)_{o\in O}\) indexes model data or variables by objects.
\(X\) and \(f\) define the feasible set and objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A permutation \(\pi\in\operatorname{Sym}(O)\) is an object-label symmetry exactly when \(\pi\cdot X=X\) and \(f(\pi\cdot x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation of object indices without changing represented values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O\) be a finite object set and let \(x=(x_o)_{o\in O}\) be an object-indexed vector. For \(\pi\in\operatorname{Sym}(O)\), define the object-label action by \((\pi\cdot x)_o=x_{\pi^{-1}(o)}\) for every \(o\in O\). The inverse ensures that \((\pi\tau)\cdot x=\pi\cdot(\tau\cdot x)\). For a feasible set \(X\) and objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), \(\pi\) is an object-label symmetry when \(\pi\cdot X=X\) and \(f(\pi\cdot x)=f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An object-label action permutes object indices while carrying their associated components; it is symmetric when the relabeled model has identical feasibility and objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Object-Label Actions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inverse-index convention correctly defines a left action and the definition fits the leaf, but the record lacks an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Relabeling Admissibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Semantic or domain distinctions that prevent otherwise algebraically plausible relabeling.

assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a proposed bijective relabeling of the model's encoded assignments.
\(X\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) are the feasible set and objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relabeling is admissible exactly when \(T(X)=X\) and \(f(Tx)=f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\); failure of either equality excludes \(T\) from the model symmetry group.

notation.meaning: Symmetry group of the optimization model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary separating valid relabeling symmetries from mere renamings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a bijection on the encoded assignment space. The relabeling belongs to the model symmetry group \(G\) if and only if \(T(X)=X\) and \(f(Tx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). Thus a value permutation is inadmissible when it violates a variable domain, a value-specific constraint, or a value-dependent objective coefficient. An object permutation is inadmissible when relabeled objects have unequal domains, parameters, incidences, or costs. Preservation of syntax alone is unnecessary, but preservation of the feasible set and objective values is mandatory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relabeling is admissible only when it preserves the feasible set and objective values; unequal domains, parameters, incidences, or costs mark the boundary of symmetry.
knowledge_statements.title: Relabeling Admissibility Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind and preservation tests fit the terminal container, but the asserted catalogue of inadmissibility causes has no cited authoritative support.

children.title: Replicated-Structure Action Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Actions on replicated blocks and indexed matrix structures.

children.title: Block Actions
children.top_down_role: Actions permuting replicated or interchangeable variable blocks.

assumptions_latex: \(x=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})\) is partitioned into blocks of equal dimension.
\(X\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) define the optimization model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A block permutation \(\pi\in S_m\) is a symmetry exactly when \(P_\pi X=X\) and \(f(P_\pi x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation of replicated variable blocks as indivisible units.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})\) consists of \(m\) equal-dimensional blocks. For \(\pi\in S_m\), define \(P_\pi x\) by \((P_\pi x)^{(k)}=x^{(\pi^{-1}(k))}\) for every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). This is a block action because all coordinates within each block move together. It is a symmetry of a model with feasible set \(X\) and objective \(f\) precisely when \(P_\pi X=X\) and \(f(P_\pi x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block action permutes equal-sized replicated variable blocks as whole units and is symmetric when the permutation preserves feasibility and objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Block Actions

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Block Actions, but the cited block-separability section does not establish that block permutations preserve a model or support the stated symmetry characterization. A symmetry-specific source is required.

children.title: Row Actions
children.top_down_role: Actions permuting interchangeable row indices in structured arrays.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq D^{m\times n}\) is a feasible set of matrix-valued assignments.
\(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is the objective function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A row permutation \(\rho\in S_m\) is a symmetry exactly when \(R_\rho X=X\) and \(f(R_\rho x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation action on interchangeable rows of a matrix-indexed model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=(x_{ij})\in D^{m\times n}\). For \(\rho\in S_m\), the row action \(R_\rho\) is defined by \((R_\rho x)_{ij}=x_{\rho^{-1}(i),j}\) for all \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). It permutes complete rows while fixing column labels. For a feasible set \(X\subseteq D^{m\times n}\) and objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), \(\rho\) is a row symmetry if and only if \(R_\rho X=X\) and \(f(R_\rho x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A row action permutes entire rows of a matrix-indexed assignment while fixing columns; interchangeable rows yield symmetries of feasibility and objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Row Actions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The row-permutation definition is internally consistent and fits the leaf, but no source with a specific locator supports it in the optimization-symmetry context.

children.title: Column Actions
children.top_down_role: Actions permuting interchangeable column indices in structured arrays.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq D^{m\times n}\) is a feasible set of matrix-valued assignments.
\(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is the objective function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A column permutation \(\kappa\in S_n\) is a symmetry exactly when \(C_\kappa X=X\) and \(f(C_\kappa x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation action on interchangeable columns of a matrix-indexed model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=(x_{ij})\in D^{m\times n}\). For \(\kappa\in S_n\), the column action \(C_\kappa\) is defined by \((C_\kappa x)_{ij}=x_{i,\kappa^{-1}(j)}\) for all \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). It permutes complete columns while fixing row labels. For a feasible set \(X\subseteq D^{m\times n}\) and objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), \(\kappa\) is a column symmetry if and only if \(C_\kappa X=X\) and \(f(C_\kappa x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A column action permutes entire columns of a matrix-indexed assignment while fixing rows; interchangeable columns yield symmetries of feasibility and objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Column Actions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The column-permutation definition is internally consistent and fits the leaf, but no source with a specific locator supports it in the optimization-symmetry context.

children.title: Binary-Domain Action Regimes
children.top_down_role: Action families whose admissibility relies on binary variable domains.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) define a binary optimization model.
\(T\) acts coordinatewise by a permutation and optional complementation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Such an action has the form \((Tx)_i=b_i+(1-2b_i)x_{\pi^{-1}(i)}\), and it is a binary-model symmetry exactly when \(T(X)=X\) and \(f(Tx)=f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate permutations combined with binary complementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), a coordinatewise signed-permutation action is specified by \(\pi\in S_n\) and \(b\in\{0,1\}^n\) through \((Tx)_i=b_i+(1-2b_i)x_{\pi^{-1}(i)}\). Thus \(b_i=0\) copies a permuted bit and \(b_i=1\) complements it. Every such \(T\) maps \(\{0,1\}^n\) bijectively to itself. It is a symmetry of the binary model with objective \(f\) precisely when \(T(X)=X\) and \(f(Tx)=f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary-domain actions may permute coordinates and independently complement bits; they are model symmetries only when feasibility and objective values remain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary-Domain Action Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation correctly describes coordinate permutations with independent binary complementations and fits the domain-regime leaf, but it is unsupported by an inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Bounded-Integer Action Regimes
children.top_down_role: Action families compatible with bounded general-integer domains.

assumptions_latex: \(D=\prod_{i=1}^n\{\ell_i,\ell_i+1,\ldots,u_i\}\) is a bounded integer box.
\(X\subseteq D\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) define the optimization model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \((Tx)_i=\ell_i+u_i-x_{\pi^{-1}(i)}\) preserves \(D\) exactly when \(\ell_i=\ell_{\pi^{-1}(i)}\) and \(u_i=u_{\pi^{-1}(i)}\) for every \(i\); it is a model symmetry when it also preserves \(X\) and \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-preserving permutations and midpoint reflections for bounded integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\prod_{i=1}^n\{\ell_i,\ell_i+1,\ldots,u_i\}\). For a permutation \(\pi\), the reflected permutation \((Tx)_i=\ell_i+u_i-x_{\pi^{-1}(i)}\) maps \(D\) onto itself if the paired coordinates have identical bounds, namely \(\ell_i=\ell_{\pi^{-1}(i)}\) and \(u_i=u_{\pi^{-1}(i)}\) for every \(i\). Pure coordinate permutations obey the same bound-matching condition. Either action is a model symmetry only if, additionally, \(T(X)=X\) and \(f(Tx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded-integer actions may permute equally bounded coordinates or reflect them about interval midpoints; model symmetry additionally requires preservation of feasibility and objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Integer Action Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound-matching condition is mathematically plausible and the condition kind fits the leaf, but no source supports the precise reflected-permutation formula and its claimed exact domain-preservation criterion.

children.title: Continuous-Domain Action Regimes
children.top_down_role: Action families acting on continuous variables while preserving modeled domain structure.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) define a continuous optimization model.
\(T(x)=Qx+d\), where \(Q\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The affine action is a model symmetry exactly when \(T(X)=X\) and \(f(Tx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\); if Euclidean geometry must also be preserved, one additionally requires \(Q^\mathsf{T}Q=I\).

notation.meaning: Nonsingular linear part of the affine action.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine actions on continuous variables, with optional Euclidean invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be the affine bijection \(T(x)=Qx+d\), where \(Q\) is nonsingular. For a continuous model with feasible set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), \(T\) is a symmetry if and only if \(T(X)=X\) and \(f(Tx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). When the intended action must preserve Euclidean distances, the additional condition is \(Q^\mathsf{T}Q=I\); permutations, rotations, and reflections are then special cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous-domain affine action is symmetric when it bijectively preserves feasibility and objective values; orthogonality is additionally required when Euclidean distances must be preserved.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Domain Action Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine symmetry condition and orthogonality qualification are coherent and fit Continuous-Domain Action Regimes, but no authoritative citation with a specific locator is provided.

children.top_down_role: Group-theoretic structures connecting global actions to variables, solutions, and search states.

children.title: Generator-Representation Interface
children.top_down_role: Compact representations used to store and process optimization symmetries.

children.title: Generator Systems
children.top_down_role: Compact generating sets used to store optimization symmetry groups.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a group acting on a set \(X\).
\(S\subseteq G\) is a specified subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is a generator system for the action exactly when \(\langle S\rangle=G\); consequently every orbit satisfies \(Gx=\{s_1^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots s_k^{\varepsilon_k}x:k\geq0,\ s_j\in S,\ \varepsilon_j\in\{-1,1\}\}\).

notation.meaning: Group acting on the model or assignment set.
Subgroup generated by the elements of the set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite descriptions of symmetry groups through generating elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) act on a set \(X\). A subset \(S\subseteq G\) is a generator system when \(\langle S\rangle=G\), meaning that every \(g\in G\) can be written as a finite product \(g=s_1^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots s_k^{\varepsilon_k}\), where \(k\geq0\), \(s_j\in S\), and \(\varepsilon_j\in\{-1,1\}\). Hence the action is determined by the maps associated with elements of \(S\), subject to the relations they satisfy, and every orbit can be generated by repeated application of these maps and their inverses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generator system is a subset whose finite products and inverses produce every group element, so its actions determine all symmetry orbits.
knowledge_statements.title: Generator Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generator-system definition is standard, precise, and appropriate for the leaf, but no group-theory or group-action source with a specific section, definition, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Permutation Representations
children.top_down_role: Representations of group actions on variables, values, or other modeled objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Permutation Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite permutation representations used to encode symmetries of optimization objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a group acting on a finite set \(\Omega\). Its permutation representation is the homomorphism \(\rho:G\to\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega)\) defined by \(\rho(g)(\omega)=g\cdot\omega\). Thus \(\rho(e)=\operatorname{id}_{\Omega}\) and \(\rho(gh)=\rho(g)\rho(h)\). After indexing \(\Omega=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), each \(\rho(g)\) is equivalently represented by a permutation matrix \(P_g\) satisfying \(P_{gh}=P_gP_h\). The representation is faithful exactly when \(\ker\rho=\{e\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite group action is encoded by a homomorphism into a symmetric group, equivalently by permutation matrices; it is faithful precisely when only the identity acts trivially.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a group acting on a finite set \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho:G\to\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega)\) is a homomorphism, with faithfulness equivalent to \(\ker\rho=\{e\}\).

notation.meaning: symmetric group of all permutations of the finite set Omega
permutation matrix representing the action of g

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation statement is mathematically standard, internally consistent, and appropriate for the leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator supports it.

children.title: Representation Conversion
children.top_down_role: Translation between generator descriptions and action representations used by optimization procedures.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion between generator maps, one-line permutations, and permutation matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite ordered set \(\Omega=\{\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_n\}\) and generator maps \(s:\Omega\to\Omega\) for \(s\in S\). For each \(s\), initialize an empty array \(p_s\); set \(p_s(i)=j\) whenever \(s(\omega_i)=\omega_j\), and reject the input if \(p_s\) is not bijective. Construct \(P_s\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) by \((P_s)_{p_s(i),i}=1\) and zero elsewhere. Stop after every \(s\in S\) is processed and output either \(\{p_s:s\in S\}\) or \(\{P_s:s\in S\}\); the inverse conversion reads the unique row containing the nonzero entry of each column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate each generator’s image of every object, verify bijectivity, and encode the resulting permutation as an array or permutation matrix; either encoding can be recovered from the other.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) and the generator set \(S\) are finite.
Each supplied generator map is evaluable on every element of \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_s e_i=e_{p_s(i)}\) for every \(s\in S\) and \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).

notation.meaning: one-line permutation induced by generator s
permutation matrix induced by generator s

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct conversion of equivalent finite permutation encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite conversion procedure is well specified, uses a consistent column-vector convention, and correctly has algorithmic content, but it has no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Optimization-Object Orbit Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Orbit structures arising on modeled objects and partial search states.

children.title: Variable Orbits
children.top_down_role: Orbit partitions of variables under the active symmetry group.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable Orbits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbits of variable indices under formulation symmetries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be the index set of variables and let \(G\) act on \(I\) by formulation-preserving permutations. The variable orbit of \(i\in I\) is \[\operatorname{Orb}_G(i)=\{g\cdot i:g\in G\}.\] Two indices \(i,j\in I\) are orbit-equivalent exactly when \(j=g\cdot i\) for some \(g\in G\). This relation partitions \(I\) into pairwise disjoint variable orbits; singleton orbits are precisely the indices fixed by every element of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable orbit contains exactly the variable indices reachable from one another by model symmetries, and all such orbits partition the variable index set.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts on the variable index set \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\) is partitioned by the sets \(\operatorname{Orb}_G(i)\).

notation.meaning: orbit of variable index i under G

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard orbit definition specialized to variable indices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and stated partition and singleton properties are correct for a group action and fit the Variable Orbits leaf, but no source locator is supplied.

children.title: Solution Orbits
children.top_down_role: Equivalence classes of feasible or optimal solutions under symmetry.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Orbits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbits of feasible solutions under objective-preserving model symmetries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the feasible set, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be the objective, and let \(G\) act on \(X\) such that \(g\cdot x\in X\) and \(f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in X\). The solution orbit of \(x\in X\) is \[\operatorname{Orb}_G(x)=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}.\] Every member of this orbit is feasible and has the same objective value; hence optimization may select an orbit representative without changing the attainable objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution orbit consists of all feasible solutions obtained from one solution by symmetries; every member has the same objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) preserves both the feasible set \(X\) and objective function \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Orb}_G(x)\subseteq X\) and \(f(y)=f(x)\) for every \(y\in\operatorname{Orb}_G(x)\).

notation.meaning: solution orbit of x under G

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard orbit definition under optimization invariance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The solution-orbit definition and invariance conclusion are correct under the explicit feasibility and objective-preservation hypotheses, but no source locator is supplied.

children.title: Search-Node Orbits
children.top_down_role: Orbit structure among partial assignments or branch-and-bound states.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Node Orbits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence classes of symmetry-related branch-and-bound subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent each search node \(u\) by its local feasible region \(X_u\subseteq X\), and let a model-symmetry group \(G\) act on node regions by \(g\cdot X_u=\{g\cdot x:x\in X_u\}\). The search-node orbit of \(u\) is \[\operatorname{Orb}_G(u)=\{v:g\cdot X_u=X_v\text{ for some }g\in G\}.\] Nodes in one orbit define isomorphic subproblems and have equal relaxation bounds whenever the relaxation construction is equivariant under \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search nodes share an orbit when a model symmetry maps one node’s local subproblem to the other; equivariant relaxations then give them equal bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) preserves the global model.
Each search node \(u\) is identified by a local region \(X_u\).
The stated bound equality requires an equivariant relaxation construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\operatorname{Orb}_G(u)\) exactly when \(X_v=g\cdot X_u\) for some \(g\in G\).

notation.meaning: local feasible region associated with search node u

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: induced group action on search subproblems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement explicitly identifies nodes by their local regions and conditions bound equality on equivariance, but this induced search-node convention and its isomorphic-subproblem claim require a supporting source.

children.title: Stabilizer Residual-Group Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Residual group structures after representative choices or search decisions.

children.title: Object Stabilizers
children.top_down_role: Residual symmetries preserving selected variables, values, or modeled objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Object Stabilizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgroups fixing a selected optimization object.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act on a set \(\Omega\), and fix \(\omega\in\Omega\). The stabilizer of \(\omega\) is \[G_\omega=\operatorname{Stab}_G(\omega)=\{g\in G:g\cdot\omega=\omega\}.\] It is a subgroup of \(G\). For a subset \(B\subseteq\Omega\), the pointwise stabilizer is \(G_{(B)}=\{g\in G:g\cdot b=b\text{ for every }b\in B\}\), whereas the setwise stabilizer is \(G_{\{B\}}=\{g\in G:g\cdot B=B\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An object stabilizer contains the group elements fixing that object; pointwise and setwise stabilizers distinguish fixing every member from preserving a subset as a whole.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts on a set \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_\omega\leq G\), \(G_{(B)}\leq G\), and \(G_{\{B\}}\leq G\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard stabilizer definitions for group actions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The object, pointwise, and setwise stabilizer definitions are standard and appropriate for the leaf, but no citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Stabilizer Chains
children.top_down_role: Nested residual-group structures associated with successive representative choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Stabilizer Chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested pointwise stabilizers induced by an ordered base.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) act on \(\Omega\), and let \(B=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_k)\) be an ordered tuple. Define \(G^{[0]}=G\) and \[G^{[i]}=\{g\in G:g\cdot\beta_j=\beta_j\text{ for }1\leq j\leq i\}\quad(1\leq i\leq k).\] Then \(G=G^{[0]}\geq G^{[1]}\geq\cdots\geq G^{[k]}\) is the stabilizer chain induced by \(B\). If \(G^{[k]}=\{e\}\), then \(B\) is a base; repeated points or redundant choices may yield non-strict inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordered sequence of objects induces a descending chain of subgroups fixing successively longer prefixes; it is a base when the final stabilizer is trivial.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts on \(\Omega\).
\(B=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_k)\) is an ordered tuple in \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G^{[i]}\leq G^{[i-1]}\) for \(1\leq i\leq k\), and \(B\) is a base when \(G^{[k]}=\{e\}\).

notation.meaning: pointwise stabilizer of the first i base points

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The descending pointwise-stabilizer chain and base condition are mathematically correct and fit the leaf, but no citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Search-Local Residual Groups
children.top_down_role: Stabilizer structures remaining after node-specific branching or fixing decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Local Residual Groups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetries remaining valid after imposing search-node restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) preserve a global feasible set \(X\), and let a search node \(u\) impose a local region \(X_u\subseteq X\). Its search-local residual group is \[G_u=\{g\in G:g\cdot X_u=X_u\}.\] Thus \(G_u\) is the setwise stabilizer of the node subproblem and is a subgroup of \(G\). If a descendant \(v\) adds restrictions to \(u\), then the symmetries deliberately retained by stabilizing all accumulated restrictions form a subgroup of \(G_u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual group at a search node consists of global symmetries preserving that node’s local subproblem; stabilizing additional descendant restrictions can only reduce the retained group.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) preserves the global feasible set \(X\).
The node region \(X_u\) completely specifies the local subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_u=\operatorname{Stab}_G(X_u)\leq G\).

notation.meaning: local feasible region at search node u
residual symmetry group at node u

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: node residual symmetry as a setwise stabilizer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual group is correctly formulated as a setwise stabilizer when the node region completely specifies the subproblem, but the search-local convention and descendant claim lack supporting evidence.

children.title: Group-Action Factorization Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Decompositions by affected variables and independently acting symmetry components.

children.title: Action Supports
children.top_down_role: Variable or object sets affected by particular symmetry elements or subgroups.

knowledge_statements.title: Action Supports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objects moved nontrivially by a permutation or subgroup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) act on a set \(\Omega\). For \(g\in G\), the support of \(g\) is \[\operatorname{supp}(g)=\{\omega\in\Omega:g\cdot\omega\neq\omega\}.\] For a subgroup \(H\leq G\), its action support is \[\operatorname{supp}(H)=\bigcup_{h\in H}\operatorname{supp}(h)=\{\omega\in\Omega:\text{some }h\in H\text{ moves }\omega\}.\] Consequently, every element of \(H\) fixes \(\Omega\setminus\operatorname{supp}(H)\) pointwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support of a permutation contains the objects it moves; a subgroup’s support is the union of the supports of all its elements.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts on \(\Omega\), and \(H\leq G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\cdot\omega=\omega\) for all \(h\in H\) and \(\omega\in\Omega\setminus\operatorname{supp}(H)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard support definition for permutation actions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The element and subgroup support definitions and pointwise-fixing consequence are correct and fit the leaf, but no citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Symmetry Components
children.top_down_role: Connected portions of the action structure identified through shared supports.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator-relative components obtained from overlapping action supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=\langle S\rangle\) act on a finite set \(\Omega\). Form the bipartite incidence graph with object vertices \(\Omega\), generator vertices \(S\), and an edge between \(\omega\in\Omega\) and \(s\in S\) exactly when \(\omega\in\operatorname{supp}(s)\). A symmetry component relative to \(S\) is the set of object vertices in a nontrivial connected component of this graph. Distinct symmetry components have no generator whose support intersects both, although the decomposition may depend on the selected generating set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to chosen generators, symmetry components are connected blocks of objects linked through overlapping generator supports; no generator acts across two distinct components.
assumptions_latex: \(G=\langle S\rangle\) acts on a finite set \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_1\neq C_2\) implies \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\) cannot intersect both \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) for any \(s\in S\).

notation.meaning: object set of a symmetry component

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: support-incidence decomposition is a common computational organizer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The incidence-graph construction is internally coherent as a generator-relative definition, but it is not a uniquely standard meaning of symmetry component; its convention and generating-set dependence require a specific source.

children.title: Independent Group Factors
children.top_down_role: Group factors acting independently on separable portions of the model.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts faithfully on \(\Omega\).
The subgroups \(H_1,\ldots,H_r\leq G\) have pairwise disjoint supports and generate \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\cong H_1\times\cdots\times H_r\) via the multiplication map \((h_1,\ldots,h_r)\mapsto h_1\cdots h_r\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: internal direct-product criterion with disjoint action supports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct-product symmetry factors acting on disjoint object supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) act faithfully on \(\Omega\). Subgroups \(H_1,\ldots,H_r\leq G\) are independent action factors when their supports are pairwise disjoint and \(G=\langle H_1,\ldots,H_r\rangle\). Pairwise disjoint supports imply that distinct factors centralize one another and have trivial intersection. Consequently, the multiplication map \[H_1\times\cdots\times H_r\to G,\qquad (h_1,\ldots,h_r)\mapsto h_1\cdots h_r\] is an isomorphism. Each factor changes only objects in its own support, so choices of factor elements combine uniquely and commute.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent factors act on pairwise disjoint supports and generate the full group; they commute, intersect trivially, and combine uniquely as an internal direct product.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Group Factors

children.title: Full Symmetric-Group Actions
children.top_down_role: Complete interchangeability within a variable or object family.

knowledge_statements.title: Full Symmetric-Group Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete interchangeability of every object within a designated family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) act on \(\Omega\), and let \(B\subseteq\Omega\) be finite. The action contains a full symmetric-group action on \(B\) if there exists a subgroup \(H\leq G\) such that every \(h\in H\) fixes \(\Omega\setminus B\) pointwise and the restriction homomorphism \(H\to\operatorname{Sym}(B)\) is an isomorphism. Equivalently, every permutation of the objects in \(B\) extends uniquely within \(H\) to a symmetry fixing all objects outside \(B\). Thus the members of \(B\) are completely interchangeable under this factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family has a full symmetric-group action when every permutation within the family is a model symmetry fixing everything outside it.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts on \(\Omega\), and \(B\subseteq\Omega\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H|_B=\operatorname{Sym}(B)\) and \(H\cong\operatorname{Sym}(B)\), with \(H\) fixing \(\Omega\setminus B\) pointwise.

notation.meaning: restriction of the subgroup action to B

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: full symmetric action characterized by restriction to an interchangeable block

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restriction-isomorphism characterization precisely captures a full symmetric-group factor acting on the designated finite family and fits the topic role, but no citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Matrix-Permutation Actions
children.top_down_role: Interchangeable rows, columns, or matrix-index blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Permutation Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row, column, and block permutations acting on matrix-indexed decision variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), let \(G_r\leq S_m\) and \(G_c\leq S_n\), and denote their permutation matrices by \(P_\sigma\) and \(Q_\tau\). The matrix-permutation action is \[(\sigma,\tau)\cdot X=P_\sigma XQ_\tau^{\mathsf T}.\] If rows or columns are partitioned into blocks, the acting groups are restricted to permutations preserving the prescribed block sizes and metadata. For a feasible set \(F\) and objective \(f\), an element is a formulation symmetry when \(X\in F\iff(\sigma,\tau)\cdot X\in F\) and \(f((\sigma,\tau)\cdot X)=f(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Row and column permutations act by left and right multiplication with permutation matrices; those preserving feasibility and objective values are formulation symmetries.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\)
\(G_r\leq S_m,\;G_c\leq S_n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\sigma,\tau)\cdot X=P_\sigma XQ_\tau^{\mathsf T}\).

notation.meaning: Permutation matrices for row and column permutations.

children.title: Rotation-Involution Action Family
children.top_down_role: Structured actions generated by rotations, reflections, or involutions.

children.title: Cyclic Actions
children.top_down_role: Structured actions generated by rotational or periodic interchangeability.

knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite cyclic permutation actions on model indices or variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\) be a finite index set and let \(\rho\in S_\Omega\) have order \(k\). The cyclic group generated by \(\rho\) is \[C_k=\langle\rho\rangle=\{e,\rho,\ldots,\rho^{k-1}\}.\] Its coordinate action on \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}\) is defined by \((\rho^t\cdot x)_i=x_{\rho^{-t}(i)}\). It is a symmetry action for a feasible set \(F\) and objective \(f\) precisely when every \(t\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}\) satisfies \(\rho^tF=F\) and \(f(\rho^t\cdot x)=f(x)\) for all \(x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-order permutation generates cyclic rotations of coordinates; it is a model symmetry when all rotations preserve feasibility and objective values.
assumptions_latex: \(|\Omega|<\infty\)
\(\rho^k=e\) with minimal \(k\geq1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_k=\langle\rho\rangle\) acts by \((\rho^t\cdot x)_i=x_{\rho^{-t}(i)}\).

notation.meaning: Symmetric group on the index set.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite cyclic coordinate action is precise and appropriate, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Dihedral Actions
children.top_down_role: Structured actions combining rotational structure with reflection structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Dihedral Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotation-reflection actions on cyclically indexed model components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\geq3\), let \(\Omega\) be a finite set, and let \(\rho,\tau\in S_\Omega\), where \(\rho\) has order \(k\), \(\tau^2=e\), and \(\tau\rho\tau=\rho^{-1}\). The generated permutation group is the dihedral group \[D_k=\langle\rho,\tau\rangle=\{\rho^t,\tau\rho^t:0\leq t<k\}.\] For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}\), each \(g\in D_k\) acts by \((g\cdot x)_i=x_{g^{-1}(i)}\). Given a feasible set \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}\) and objective \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\), this is a formulation-symmetry action exactly when \(gF=F\) and \(f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in D_k\) and \(x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A permutation of order k and an involution that reverses it generate a dihedral coordinate action; the action is a formulation symmetry exactly when every group element preserves feasibility and objective values.
assumptions_latex: \(k\geq3\)
\(|\Omega|<\infty\)
\(\operatorname{ord}(\rho)=k\)
\(\tau\rho\tau=\rho^{-1}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_k=\{\rho^t,\tau\rho^t:0\leq t<k\}\) acts by coordinate permutations.

notation.meaning: Dihedral group consisting of k rotations and k reflections.
Symmetric group on the finite set Omega.

children.title: Involutive Actions
children.top_down_role: Order-two transformations arising from swaps, reversals, or reflections.

knowledge_statements.title: Involutive Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-two transformations representing swaps, reflections, or sign reversals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\tau:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(\tau\circ\tau=\operatorname{id}\). Then \(\{e,\tau\}\) defines an involutive action. It is a symmetry of the optimization model exactly when \[x\in F\iff\tau(x)\in F,\qquad f(\tau(x))=f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in F.\] Coordinate swaps, centered sign reversals, and geometric reflections are instances whenever they also preserve variable domains and all model data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An involution is a transformation whose square is the identity; it is a model symmetry when it preserves domains, feasibility, and objective values.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
\(\tau^2=\operatorname{id}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{e,\tau\}\) is a symmetry group if \(\tau(F)=F\) and \(f\circ\tau=f\) on \(F\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise and fits the involutive-actions leaf, but it has no source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Composite Action Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Layered interchangeability among objects and their interchangeable subobjects.

children.title: Direct-Product Actions
children.top_down_role: Independent symmetry actions on disjoint or separable object families.

knowledge_statements.title: Direct-Product Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent group actions on disjoint blocks of model coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega=\Omega_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}\Omega_r\), and suppose \(G_j\) acts on \(\Omega_j\). The direct product \(G=G_1\times\cdots\times G_r\) acts componentwise: for \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_r)\) and \(i\in\Omega_j\), \[g(i)=g_j(i),\qquad (g\cdot x)_i=x_{g_j^{-1}(i)}.\] The factors commute because their supports are disjoint. If each extended factor action preserves a feasible set \(F\), an objective \(f\), and the coordinate domains, then the entire direct-product action preserves them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent symmetry groups on disjoint coordinate blocks combine into a direct-product action, with each factor moving only its own block.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{j=1}^r\Omega_j\)
\(G_j\curvearrowright\Omega_j\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_1\times\cdots\times G_r\) acts independently on the disjoint blocks \(\Omega_j\).

children.title: Wreath-Product Actions
children.top_down_role: Layered actions coupling interchangeable blocks with interchangeable contents.

knowledge_statements.title: Wreath-Product Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Within-block symmetries combined with permutations of interchangeable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) act on \(\Omega\), and let \(K\leq S_b\) permute \(b\) copies of \(\Omega\). The imprimitive wreath product is \[H\wr K=H^b\rtimes K.\] For \((h_1,\ldots,h_b;k)\in H\wr K\), its action on \(\Omega\times\{1,\ldots,b\}\) first applies \(h_j\) inside block \(j\) and then sends that block to \(k(j)\): \[(\omega,j)\longmapsto(h_j\omega,k(j)).\] Thus the action represents independent within-block transformations together with permutations of structurally identical blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A wreath product combines independent symmetries inside identical blocks with a group that permutes the blocks themselves.
assumptions_latex: \(H\curvearrowright\Omega\)
\(K\leq S_b\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\wr K=H^b\rtimes K\) acts imprimitively on \(\Omega\times\{1,\ldots,b\}\).

notation.meaning: Direct product of b copies of the within-block group.

children.title: Nested Action Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Multilevel interchangeability among objects containing interchangeable subobjects.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Action Hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry actions organized by recursively nested coordinate partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P_0\preceq\mathcal P_1\preceq\cdots\preceq\mathcal P_d\) be partitions of a finite coordinate set \(\Omega\), where each block of \(\mathcal P_{\ell}\) lies in one block of \(\mathcal P_{\ell+1}\). A nested action hierarchy is a subgroup \[G\leq\{g\in S_\Omega:g(B)\in\mathcal P_\ell\text{ for every }B\in\mathcal P_\ell\text{ and every }\ell\}.\] Local actions may permute coordinates inside leaf blocks and interchange isomorphic child blocks, but every generator preserves the entire partition chain. Iterated direct or wreath products provide representations when the corresponding substructures are independent or interchangeable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested hierarchy preserves every level of a refinement chain while permitting local symmetries and exchanges of structurally identical child blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(|\Omega|<\infty\)
\(\mathcal P_0\preceq\cdots\preceq\mathcal P_d\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) preserves each partition \(\mathcal P_\ell\) setwise.

children.title: Linear-Constraint Detection Graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Constraint Detection Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Colored incidence encoding for detecting symmetries of linear mixed-integer formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a formulation \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\mathrel{\bowtie}b,\;\ell\leq x\leq u,\;x_i\in D_i\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), construct a colored bipartite graph \(G\) with variable vertices \(v_i\), row vertices \(r_j\), and an edge \(v_ir_j\) exactly when \(A_{ji}\neq0\). Give the two vertex classes distinct type colors. Refine variable colors by \((c_i,\ell_i,u_i,D_i)\), row colors by \((b_j,\bowtie_j)\), and edge colors by \(A_{ji}\). Every color-preserving automorphism of \(G\) induces simultaneous column and row permutations preserving all explicitly encoded formulation data and therefore induces a formulation symmetry. Exact numerical values must receive distinct colors unless a sound normalization is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A colored variable-row incidence graph uses distinct colors for the two vertex classes and encodes coefficients, bounds, domains, row senses, right-hand sides, and objective data; its color-preserving automorphisms induce symmetries of the encoded linear formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\)
\(D_i\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{Z},\{0,1\}\}\)
Variable and row vertices have distinct type colors
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{col}}(G)\) induces row and column permutations preserving the encoded linear formulation.

notation.meaning: Sense of row j: less than or equal to, equality, or greater than or equal to.

children.title: Expression Detection Graphs
