knowledge_statements.title: Expression Detection Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Colored directed acyclic graphs encoding nonlinear expressions and variable metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent each objective or constraint expression by a colored directed acyclic graph. Leaves represent variables or constants; internal vertices represent operator occurrences; and an arc from an argument to its operator records data dependence. Vertex colors encode variable domains and bounds, constant values, operator symbols, and arities. Argument positions are additionally colored for noncommutative operators, while interchangeable arguments of commutative operators may share a color. A color-preserving graph automorphism that also preserves expression-root types induces a variable permutation preserving the represented expression system syntactically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A colored expression DAG records variables, constants, operators, and argument order; its admissible automorphisms reveal syntactic symmetries of the represented model.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite directed acyclic graph
Every noncommutative argument position is encoded
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{col}}(G)\) preserves the encoded expression system syntactically.

source_refs.locator: Using expression graphs in optimization algorithms p. 247

source_witnesses.locator: Using expression graphs in optimization algorithms p. 247

children.title: Operator Detection Graphs
children.top_down_role: Graph encodings preserving operator types, argument roles, or handler-specific structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Detection Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-centered encoding of expression structure for symmetry detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given expression directed acyclic graphs, form an operator detection graph whose principal vertices are operator occurrences. Color each principal vertex by operator symbol, arity, and relevant algebraic attributes such as commutativity. Join two operator vertices by a directed edge when the output of the first is an argument of the second; encode the receiving argument position whenever order matters. Attach colored boundary vertices for variable and constant arguments. Any color- and direction-preserving automorphism preserves operator types, dependency structure, ordered arguments, and boundary metadata, and therefore induces a syntactic automorphism of the encoded operator network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator graph retains operator types, dependencies, argument positions, and variable boundaries; admissible automorphisms preserve this computational structure.
assumptions_latex: The represented expressions are finite and acyclic
Operator arities and ordered arguments are encoded
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{col}}(G_{\mathrm{op}})\) preserves the encoded operator network.

source_refs.locator: Using expression graphs in optimization algorithms p. 247

source_witnesses.locator: Using expression graphs in optimization algorithms p. 247

children.title: Expression-Operator Incidence Structure
children.top_down_role: Connections between expression nodes and structured operators used to constrain admissible automorphisms.

knowledge_statements.title: Expression-Operator Incidence Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite interface linking model expressions to their operator occurrences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) index objective and constraint expressions and let \(O\) index operator occurrences in their shared expression directed acyclic graph. Define the colored bipartite incidence structure \(B=(E\mathbin{\dot\cup}O,I)\) by \[(e,o)\in I\iff o\text{ lies in the subgraph rooted at expression }e.\] Expression vertices are colored by objective or constraint role and constraint sense; operator vertices are colored by symbol and arity. If shared subexpressions are retained, one operator may be incident with several expressions. Color-preserving automorphisms of \(B\) preserve expression membership and operator classes, but must be intersected with automorphisms preserving the internal expression dependencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The incidence structure records which operator occurrences belong to each objective or constraint, including operators shared across expressions.
assumptions_latex: \(|E|<\infty\)
\(|O|<\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B=(E\mathbin{\dot\cup}O,I)\) records expression-to-operator membership.

notation.meaning: Set of objective and constraint expressions.

source_refs.locator: Using expression graphs in optimization algorithms p. 247

source_witnesses.locator: Using expression graphs in optimization algorithms p. 247

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf and correctly notes that incidence automorphisms alone do not preserve internal dependencies, but the custom transitive-membership incidence structure is not supported by the cited expression-graph locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Signed-Action Detection Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired-literal graph encoding for detecting reflections and signed coordinate permutations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose centers \(c_i\) and write \(y_i=x_i-c_i\). Create paired literal vertices \(v_i^+\) and \(v_i^-\), representing \(y_i\) and \(-y_i\), and connect each pair by a uniquely colored pairing edge. Encode constraints, objective terms, domains, and centered bounds using colored incidence vertices and edges, with signs represented by the selected literal. Any color-preserving automorphism that maps literal pairs to literal pairs induces \[y_i\longmapsto s_i y_{\pi(i)},\qquad s_i\in\{-1,1\}.\] It is a valid model symmetry only if direct substitution preserves every original domain, constraint, and objective term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Paired positive and negative literals let graph automorphisms propose signed permutations; substitution into the full model is required for validation.
assumptions_latex: \(y_i=x_i-c_i\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Admissible pair-preserving automorphisms induce \(y_i\mapsto s_i y_{\pi(i)}\).

notation.meaning: Paired vertices representing opposite centered literals.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The paired-literal proposal plausibly exposes signed permutations and appropriately requires substitution validation, but no source supports the encoding, pairing constraints, or centering conventions.

children.title: Combinatorial Automorphism Detection
children.top_down_role: Detection inherited from underlying graphs, incidence systems, or combinatorial designs.

assumptions_latex: The integer model has variables indexed by a finite set \(V\) and combinatorial data represented by a finite colored relational structure \(\mathcal C\).
Every color distinguishes objects whose optimization roles or data are not interchangeable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each accepted induced permutation belongs to the model-symmetry group.

notation.meaning: Colored combinatorial structure encoding the model
Automorphism group of the colored structure

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: colored-structure automorphisms are the standard representation for detecting combinatorial symmetries
source_needed: supplied locators do not directly document the complete detection-and-validation rule
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite colored graph or incidence-structure detection followed by explicit model validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a colored encoding \(\mathcal C\) of variables, constraints, coefficients, incidence relations, and combinatorial objects. Initialize \(G=\{e\}\). Compute generators of \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal C)\); for each generator, restrict its action to \(V\). Retain the induced permutation only if it preserves variable domains, the feasible set, and objective values. Stop after all generators have been tested and output the group generated by the retained permutations. The coloring must separate every optimization role that is required to remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encode the model as a colored combinatorial structure, compute its automorphisms, induce variable permutations, and retain only permutations that preserve domains, feasibility, and objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Automorphism Detection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and its algorithm content kind fit the detection leaf, and the retained generators do generate only valid model symmetries. However, no citation supports the colored encoding, automorphism computation, or validation rule, and the procedure is not stated as an exhaustive computation of all model symmetries. An authoritative symmetry-detection source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Matrix-Orbitope Recognition Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Recognition of interchangeable matrix indices and orbitopal subgroup structure.

children.title: Matrix-Symmetry Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of interchangeable row, column, or block indices in matrix-structured variables.

assumptions_latex: The model contains a matrix \(X=(x_{ij})\) with rows indexed by \(I\) and columns indexed by \(J\).
Columns proposed as interchangeable have identical domains and identical coefficient and incidence data outside their column labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proposed column-permutation group acts by model symmetries.
review_flags: source_scope_indirect: matrix-block locator supports matrix organization but may not state symmetry recognition explicitly
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition of column permutations in a matrix-variable substructure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A group \(G\leq S_J\) is recognized as a matrix symmetry group when, for every \(\pi\in G\), the substitution \(x_{ij}\mapsto x_{i,\pi(j)}\) preserves every variable domain, constraint function and right-hand side, and the objective function. Recognition requires the same permutation to act consistently on all occurrences of each column and requires any nonmatrix data attached to a column to be carried to identical data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Columns form a recognized matrix symmetry exactly when every proposed column permutation consistently preserves domains, all constraints, the objective, and attached column data.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Symmetry Recognition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically coherent and fits matrix-symmetry recognition, but the cited matrix-block modeling section does not directly support recognition of a column-permutation symmetry group. A specific source on formulation or matrix symmetries is required.

children.title: Orbitope Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of orbitopal subgroup structure in binary or general-domain matrix models.

assumptions_latex: The variables form a binary matrix \(X\in\{0,1\}^{p\times q}\).
The full symmetric group \(S_q\) acts on columns and preserves the optimization model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Lexicographically maximal column representatives lie in the corresponding packing, partitioning, or full orbitope.
review_flags: source_needed: an authoritative orbitope definition or recognition result with a specific locator is required
standard_field_rationale: orbitopes are convex hulls of lexicographically ordered binary matrices under column permutations
notation_repaired: malformed column notation replaced by X_{\bullet j}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary column-permutation orbitopes with lexicographically maximal representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An orbitopal structure is recognized when feasible matrices are invariant under all column permutations and the intended canonical representatives satisfy \(X_{\bullet 1}\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}\cdots\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}X_{\bullet q}\). If each row has at most one entry equal to \(1\), the recognized object is a packing orbitope; if each row has exactly one entry equal to \(1\), it is a partitioning orbitope; without either row-sum restriction, it is the full column-permutation orbitope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary matrix admits orbitopal treatment when all columns are interchangeable and canonical representatives are obtained by lexicographically ordering them, with the orbitope variant determined by row-sum restrictions.
knowledge_statements.title: Orbitope Recognition

children.title: Orbitopal Recognition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural features that support or obstruct identification of orbitopal action regimes.

assumptions_latex: A proposed matrix symmetry acts on columns of \(X=(x_{ij})\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outside the stated boundary, standard column-orbitope restrictions need not preserve an optimal representative from every orbit.
review_flags: source_needed: supplied locators do not state orbitopal applicability boundaries
standard_field_rationale: standard orbitopes require a genuine uniform column action and compatible matrix domains
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of standard binary column-orbitope recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Standard binary column-orbitope recognition fails if \(G\) is not the asserted uniform column-permutation group, if a column permutation changes domains, constraints, objective data, or side information, or if the action mixes entries in a way not expressible as \(x_{ij}\mapsto x_{i,\pi(j)}\). Packing or partitioning recognition additionally fails when the respective row conditions \(\sum_j x_{ij}\leq 1\) or \(\sum_j x_{ij}=1\) are absent. In these cases, imposing the corresponding standard orbitope may delete entire feasible or optimal orbits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard orbitopes are inapplicable when symmetry is not a uniform compatible column action or when required binary and row-sum conditions fail; imposing them may remove valid orbits.
knowledge_statements.title: Orbitopal Recognition Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no source supports the applicability limits. In addition, merely omitting an explicit row-sum constraint does not establish failure if the same row property follows from other constraints; the boundary must be stated in terms of whether feasible matrices satisfy the relevant row condition. Source-supported correction is required.

children.title: Replicated-Block Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition of interchangeable scenarios, units, stages, or submodels.

assumptions_latex: Variables and constraints are partitioned into blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\) with common local index sets.
Coupling data are invariant under a proposed permutation of the block indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted block permutations generate symmetries of the complete model.
review_flags: source_scope_indirect: block-separability sources support block structure but require confirmation for symmetry recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detection of interchangeable scenarios, units, stages, or submodels.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\), their local domains and coefficients, and all coupling incidences. Initialize a colored signature for each block from its local algebraic data. Refine signatures using coupling data until no signature changes. For each permutation among blocks with equal stable signatures, test whether the simultaneous relabeling of local variables and constraints preserves domains, all local and coupling constraints, and the objective. Stop after all generators are tested and output the group generated by accepted block permutations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refine blocks by local and coupling data, propose permutations only among matching blocks, and retain those whose simultaneous relabeling preserves the entire optimization model.
knowledge_statements.title: Replicated-Block Recognition

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An algorithm is appropriate for replicated-block recognition, and final whole-model validation is mathematically sound. The statement shifts between testing every permutation and testing generators without defining the proposed group or generator set. The cited block-structure sections do not directly support this symmetry-recognition algorithm, so an authoritative source and a precise candidate-generation specification are required.

children.title: Symmetry Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks separating valid optimization symmetries from superficial similarities in a representation.

children.title: Optimization-Role Compatibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Validation of the modeled optimization roles affected by a proposed action.

children.title: Objective Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Validation that a proposed action preserves the modeled objective role.

assumptions_latex: The model minimizes or maximizes an objective \(f:D\to\mathbb R\).
A proposed variable permutation \(g:D\to D\) is bijective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equality \(f(gx)=f(x)\) certifies objective compatibility of \(g\).
review_flags: source_scope_indirect: general integer-programming model locator requires confirmation for the symmetry certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise invariance certificate for the optimization objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proposed permutation \(g\) is objective-compatible precisely when \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in D\). For a linear objective \(f(x)=c^\top x+c_0\) and permutation matrix \(P_g\), this condition is certified by \(P_g^\top c=c\). A submitted certificate consists of the permutation and either the functional identity or the coefficient equality, both of which are directly checkable from the model data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A permutation is objective-compatible when it leaves every objective value unchanged; for a linear objective, invariance of the coefficient vector is a directly checkable certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the terminal container, and both the functional identity and the linear coefficient test are precise. The cited general integer-programming-model chapter does not directly support an objective-symmetry certificate. A symmetry-specific source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Constraint-System Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Validation that a proposed action preserves the constraint system and constraint roles.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(F=\{x\in D:h_i(x)\leq0\ (i\in I),\ h_i(x)=0\ (i\in E)\}\).
A proposed permutation \(g:D\to D\) is bijective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identity \(g(F)=F\) certifies constraint-system compatibility.
review_flags: source_scope_indirect: general model locator requires confirmation for constraint-system symmetry validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Setwise invariance certificate for the complete constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Constraint-system compatibility of \(g\) is certified by \(x\in F\Longleftrightarrow gx\in F\) for every \(x\in D\), equivalently \(g(F)=F\). A syntactic certificate may give a permutation \(\sigma\) of constraint indices such that each transformed constraint \(h_i(g^{-1}x)\) equals \(h_{\sigma(i)}(x)\), while preserving inequality versus equality sense and every right-hand side. The certificate must include all constraints, including linking and global constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A permutation is constraint-compatible when it maps the feasible set onto itself; matching every transformed constraint to an identical constraint provides a finite syntactic certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-System Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The setwise invariance condition is correct and the certificate kind fits the leaf. The syntactic matching condition is a sufficient finite certificate, as stated. The cited general modeling chapter does not directly document constraint-system symmetry validation, so a specific supporting source is required.

children.title: Optimization-Role Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Joint consistency of a proposed action across objective and feasibility structures.

assumptions_latex: The model has feasible set \(F\subseteq D\), objective \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and proposed bijection \(g:D\to D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two invariance identities certify that \(g\) maps every feasible solution to an objective-equivalent feasible solution.
review_flags: source_scope_indirect: general model locator requires confirmation for the combined optimization-role certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined feasibility and objective-value validation of a candidate symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A candidate transformation \(g\) is compatible with its optimization role when both \(g(F)=F\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). A certificate consists of independently checkable constraint-system and objective-compatibility certificates for the same transformation. These identities imply that \(g\) preserves feasibility, objective values, and hence the partition of \(F\) into solution orbits containing either only optimal points or no optimal points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate symmetry is optimization-role compatible when the same transformation preserves both the feasible set and all feasible objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Role Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The combined certificate correctly requires feasible-set and feasible-objective invariance for the same bijection and fits the exact terminal container. The supplied general integer-programming locator does not directly support this model-symmetry criterion. A symmetry-specific citation is required.

children.title: Variable-Domain Compatibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Validation across variable domains, bounds, and discrete or continuous types.

children.title: Domain Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of proposed transformations with admissible variable domains.

assumptions_latex: The variable domain is a Cartesian product \(D=\prod_{i=1}^n D_i\).
A permutation \(\pi\in S_n\) acts by \((P_\pi x)_i=x_{\pi^{-1}(i)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equalities \(D_i=D_{\pi(i)}\) for all \(i\) certify \(P_\pi(D)=D\).
review_flags: source_scope_indirect: integer-programming model locator requires confirmation for domain invariance under permutations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-domain invariance under a coordinate permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Domain compatibility of \(\pi\) means \(P_\pi(D)=D\). For the product domain \(D=\prod_{i=1}^n D_i\), it is certified by \(D_i=D_{\pi(i)}\) for every \(i\). Each \(D_i\) includes all declared restrictions on coordinate \(i\), such as integrality, admissible discrete values, intervals, and fixed values. Equality only of coefficient patterns is insufficient when the corresponding coordinate domains differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate permutation is domain-compatible exactly when it maps the full product domain onto itself, which follows by matching every permuted coordinate's complete declared domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-domain criterion is mathematically correct for the stated coordinate action, and the certificate kind fits the leaf. The cited general integer-programming-model chapter does not directly support domain invariance under coordinate permutations. A specific supporting locator is required.

children.title: Bound Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of proposed transformations with lower, upper, or fixed bounds.

assumptions_latex: Each variable satisfies \(l_i\leq x_i\leq u_i\), where endpoints may be infinite.
A permutation \(\pi\in S_n\) acts on variable indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Matching lower and upper bounds certifies invariance of the bound box.

notation.meaning: Lower and upper bounds of variable i

review_flags: source_scope_indirect: general integer-programming model locator requires confirmation for bound compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise lower- and upper-bound invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Bound compatibility of \(\pi\) is certified by \(l_i=l_{\pi(i)}\) and \(u_i=u_{\pi(i)}\) for every \(i\), with equality interpreted in the extended real line. Equivalently, the coordinate permutation satisfies \(P_\pi(B)=B\) for \(B=\prod_i[l_i,u_i]\). Fixed variables, represented by \(l_i=u_i\), may therefore be exchanged only with variables fixed at the same value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable permutation preserves bounds when every exchanged pair has identical lower and upper bounds, including infinities and fixed values.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound-matching certificate is precise, handles infinite endpoints and fixed variables, and fits the terminal container. The cited source is only a general model chapter and does not directly support permutation-based bound compatibility. A more specific source is required.

children.title: Variable-Type Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility across binary, general-integer, semicontinuous, or continuous variable types.

assumptions_latex: Each coordinate has a declared type \(\tau_i\in\{\mathrm{continuous},\mathrm{integer},\mathrm{binary},\mathrm{semicontinuous},\mathrm{semiinteger}\}\).
A permutation \(\pi\in S_n\) acts on variable indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identities \(\tau_i=\tau_{\pi(i)}\) certify preservation of variable types.
review_flags: source_scope_indirect: general integer-programming model locator requires confirmation for type-preserving permutations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of declared variable classes under permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Variable-type compatibility of \(\pi\) is certified by \(\tau_i=\tau_{\pi(i)}\) for every coordinate \(i\). For binary variables, the declaration and the domain \(\{0,1\}\) must both be preserved when solver behavior depends on the declaration. Matching types is necessary but not by itself sufficient for domain compatibility: bounds, admissible value sets, and other coordinate restrictions must also agree along each cycle of \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A permutation is type-compatible when it exchanges only variables with identical declarations; matching types alone does not ensure that bounds or other domain restrictions agree.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Type Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly distinguishes type compatibility from full domain compatibility, and certificate is the appropriate content kind. The cited general modeling chapter does not directly support type-preserving symmetry validation. A specific symmetry or solver-modeling source is required.

children.title: Semantic-Data Compatibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Validation of modeled objects whose algebraic similarity may conceal distinct application roles.

children.title: Semantic Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Validation that exchanged objects have interchangeable application roles.

assumptions_latex: Each variable and constraint has a semantic role label from a set \(R\).
A proposed transformation \(g\) induces permutations of variables and constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Preservation of all role labels and role-dependent data certifies semantic compatibility.
review_flags: source_needed: supplied locators do not define a formal semantic-role compatibility certificate
standard_field_rationale: semantic metadata must be invariant whenever it affects interpretation or downstream model use
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validation of role metadata not fully represented by algebraic coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho\) assign each model object a role in \(R\), together with role-dependent metadata. A transformation \(g\) is semantically compatible when \(\rho(gv)=\rho(v)\) for every variable and transformed constraints retain their original roles, and when all role-dependent data are carried to identical data. A certificate lists the induced object permutations and verifies these equalities. Algebraic invariance alone is insufficient whenever names encode time, ownership, scenario identity, physical units, or externally imposed distinctions that constrain valid interchangeability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transformation is semantically compatible when it preserves every role label and all role-dependent metadata; algebraic symmetry alone is insufficient when external meanings restrict interchangeability.
knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A certificate is appropriate for this semantic-validation leaf, but the role-label framework and the distinction between interpretation-only metadata and data that constrain valid optimization symmetries are not sourced. The transformation's action on all labeled model objects also needs a source-supported formal specification before the certificate can be relied upon.

children.title: Data Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Validation that coefficients, attributes, or instance data support the proposed exchange.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite set of modeled entities, and \(d_i\) is the complete exogenous-data signature relevant to entity \(i\).
\(\pi:I\to I\) is a candidate permutation produced by algebraic symmetry detection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\) is data-compatible exactly when \(d_{\pi(i)}=d_i\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility concerns all exogenous attributes whose preservation is required by the intended integer model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be the entity index set and let \(d_i\) collect every exogenous attribute of entity \(i\) that affects admissibility, costs, capacities, or interpretation. A candidate permutation \(\pi:I\to I\) is data-compatible when
\[
 d_{\pi(i)}=d_i\qquad\text{for every }i\in I.
\]
Equality is componentwise and includes attributes stored outside the algebraic coefficient arrays whenever those attributes define the intended optimization instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A detected permutation is data-compatible when it preserves every exogenous attribute relevant to feasibility, cost, capacity, or interpretation.
knowledge_statements.title: Data Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the Data Compatibility leaf and is mathematically coherent, but no inspectable source supports the proposed complete-data-signature criterion.

children.title: Algebraic-Semantic Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Cases where algebraic similarity conceals distinctions relevant to the modeled application.

assumptions_latex: \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) assigns job \(i\) to machine \(j\in\{1,2\}\).
The encoded capacities and costs are identical for machines 1 and 2, but an omitted semantic eligibility relation satisfies \(E_1\ne E_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The column swap is an algebraic symmetry of the encoding but not a symmetry of the intended assignment problem.

notation.meaning: Jobs semantically eligible for machine j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete mismatch caused by semantic data omitted from an otherwise symmetric algebraic encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an assignment encoding with variables \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) and identical encoded costs and capacities for machines \(1\) and \(2\). Its constraints and objective are invariant under \(x_{i1}\leftrightarrow x_{i2}\). Suppose, however, that the intended instance has eligibility sets \(E_1\ne E_2\), and these sets were omitted from the encoding. Swapping the machine columns can then map a semantically permitted assignment to a prohibited one. Thus algebraic invariance alone does not certify semantic symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical encoded machine columns may be swappable even though omitted eligibility data distinguish the machines, invalidating the swap for the intended problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic-Semantic Mismatch

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample fits the mismatch leaf and is internally coherent, but it has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Detection Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by representation choice, numerical conventions, and detection resources.

children.title: Transformation-Dependent Detection Boundary
children.top_down_role: Dependence of detected groups on transformations and auxiliary representations.

children.title: Presolve Dependence
children.top_down_role: Changes in detected symmetry caused by variable elimination, aggregation, or constraint processing.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is the binary model \(x_1+x_2=1\).
Presolve substitutes \(x_2=1-x_1\), producing a one-variable representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original coordinate swap need not remain detectable as a coordinate permutation after presolve.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detection is representation-dependent even when presolve preserves the optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the binary model
\[
 x_1+x_2=1,
\]
the transposition \(x_1\leftrightarrow x_2\) is an exact coordinate symmetry. A valid presolve may eliminate \(x_2\) by setting \(x_2=1-x_1\). In the resulting one-variable model, the induced symmetry is the affine map \(x_1\mapsto1-x_1\), not a permutation of remaining coordinates. Consequently, a coordinate-permutation detector can report different symmetry groups before and after equivalent presolve transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Presolve can convert a visible coordinate permutation into a non-permutation transformation, so detected symmetry depends on the presolved representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Presolve Dependence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary classification and example fit Presolve Dependence, but the representation-dependent detection claim lacks cited support.

children.title: Reformulation Dependence
children.top_down_role: Changes in detected symmetry caused by lifting, auxiliary variables, or alternative encodings.

assumptions_latex: The reformulation substitutes \(x_1=y\) and \(x_2=1-y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalent formulations can expose different groups to detectors restricted to coordinate permutations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The boundary concerns formulation-visible coordinate symmetries, not equivalence of feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
 F=\{x\in\{0,1\}^2:x_1+x_2=1\},
\]
the swap \((x_1,x_2)\mapsto(x_2,x_1)\) is a coordinate permutation. Under the equivalent substitution \(x_1=y\), \(x_2=1-y\), the same action becomes \(y\mapsto1-y\). Since this is not a permutation of variables in the reformulated model, a detector restricted to coordinate permutations may find the symmetry in the original formulation but not in the substituted formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equivalent reformulation may turn a coordinate swap into an affine action, changing what a permutation-based detector discovers.
knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation Dependence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly illustrates reformulation-dependent visibility to coordinate-permutation detectors, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Cross-Stage Symmetry Stability
children.top_down_role: Persistence of detected groups across original, presolved, or reformulated model stages.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts by exact symmetries on a model domain \(X\).
Each stage map \(T_s:X_s\to X_{s+1}\) has an associated injective homomorphism \(\rho_s:G_s\to G_{s+1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(T_s(gx)=\rho_s(g)T_s(x)\) at every stage, the represented symmetry action is stable across the pipeline.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability is expressed by equivariant stage transformations and faithful transport of group actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G_s\) act on the stage domain \(X_s\). Symmetry is stable from stage \(s\) to \(s+1\) when there is an injective homomorphism \(\rho_s:G_s\to G_{s+1}\) such that
\[
 T_s(gx)=\rho_s(g)T_s(x)
 \quad\text{for all }g\in G_s,
 \quad x\in X_s.
\]
Cross-stage stability holds when this equivariance condition is satisfied at every transformation stage; injectivity prevents distinct detected symmetries from being collapsed during transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetry is stable across stages when every transformation intertwines the group actions and transports distinct symmetries injectively.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Stage Symmetry Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf, but injective equivariant transport is a particular formalization of cross-stage stability and requires an authoritative source or an explicitly justified local convention.

children.title: Symmetry Exactness Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Boundary between exact group actions and tolerance-based or heuristic similarity.

children.title: Exact Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Group actions supported by exact preservation of the relevant model structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimization symmetry preserves both feasibility and objective values without tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimization model with feasible set \(F\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^q\) and objective \(f:F\to\mathbb R\), an integrality-type-preserving bijection \(g\) is an exact symmetry when
\[
g(F)=F
\quad\text{and}\quad
f(gx)=f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in F.
\]
A collection of such transformations is an exact symmetry group when it contains the identity and is closed under composition and inversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact symmetry bijectively preserves the feasible set and leaves every feasible solution's objective value unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^q\) is the feasible set of a minimization model with objective \(f:F\to\mathbb R\).
\(g\) is a bijection of the ambient variable domain preserving integrality types.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is exact precisely when \(g(F)=F\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\).

children.title: Approximate Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Near-invariant structure treated through explicit similarity tolerances or heuristic criteria.

assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a bounded variable domain, \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and \(r:D\to\mathbb R^m\) is a normalized constraint-residual map.
\(g:D\to D\) is a bijection preserving variable types, and \(\varepsilon_f,\varepsilon_r\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is approximately symmetric when its worst objective and residual perturbations do not exceed \(\varepsilon_f\) and \(\varepsilon_r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A residual-based quantitative definition; normalization must be fixed before tolerances are interpreted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be bounded, let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and let \(r:D\to\mathbb R^m\) be a fixed normalized residual representation of all constraints. A type-preserving bijection \(g:D\to D\) is an \((\varepsilon_f,\varepsilon_r)\)-approximate symmetry when
\[
 \sup_{x\in D}|f(gx)-f(x)|\le\varepsilon_f,
 \qquad
 \sup_{x\in D}\|r(gx)-r(x)\|_\infty\le\varepsilon_r.
\]
The definition depends on the stated residual normalization and does not by itself imply exact preservation of feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate symmetry bounds the worst objective and normalized constraint-residual changes caused by a transformation over a fixed domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Symmetry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is explicit and appropriately warns that feasibility need not be preserved, but this residual-based notion is normalization- and norm-dependent and has no source establishing it as the intended Approximate Symmetry notion.

children.title: Numerical Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Apparent symmetry whose recognition depends on floating-point representation or numerical tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical symmetry is an encoding-level tolerance classification rather than exact invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For scalars, define \(a\approx_\tau b\) by
\[
|a-b|\le \tau_a+\tau_r\max\{|a|,|b|\},
\]
and apply this predicate componentwise to conformable arrays. Consider an encoded model with matrix \(A\), row data \(b\), objective vector \(c\), bounds \(l,u\), and variable and row types. Let \(P\) be a type-preserving variable-permutation matrix and \(Q\) a row-permutation matrix preserving row types. The pair \((P,Q)\) is a numerical symmetry candidate when
\[
QAP^{\mathsf T}\approx_\tau A,
\quad Qb\approx_\tau b,
\quad Pc\approx_\tau c,
\quad Pl\approx_\tau l,
\quad Pu\approx_\tau u.
\]
These tests depend on scaling and tolerances and do not certify exact feasibility or objective invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerical symmetry candidate uses compatible variable and constraint permutations that preserve encoded coefficients, row data, objective coefficients, and bounds within fixed absolute-relative tolerances; this does not certify exact invariance.
assumptions_latex: A finite encoded model has numerical data \((A,b,c,l,u)\) together with row and variable types.
\(P\) is a type-preserving variable-permutation matrix, \(Q\) is a row-permutation matrix preserving row types, and componentwise comparison tolerances \(\tau_a,\tau_r\ge 0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Passing the stated tolerance tests makes \((P,Q)\) a numerical symmetry candidate, not necessarily an exact model symmetry.

notation.meaning: Permutation matrix acting on constraint rows

children.title: Partial Generator Discovery
children.top_down_role: Incomplete symmetry information arising from restricted encodings or computation limits.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is the exact symmetry group of a model.
A detection procedure returns generators \(S\subseteq G\) and the generated subgroup \(H=\langle S\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Symmetry handling based on \(H\) is valid for \(H\)-orbits but incomplete whenever \(H\subsetneq G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The statement separates validity of discovered generators from completeness of group discovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be the full exact symmetry group and let a detector return a validated set \(S\subseteq G\). Then \(H=\langle S\rangle\) is a subgroup of \(G\). Any representative-selection constraint proved valid for every \(H\)-orbit remains valid for the discovered action. If \(H\subsetneq G\), however, distinct \(H\)-orbits can lie in one \(G\)-orbit, so the procedure can retain multiple solutions that are symmetric under undiscovered elements of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validated partial generators define a safe subgroup, but symmetry reduction is incomplete when that subgroup is smaller than the full symmetry group.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial Generator Discovery

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits Partial Generator Discovery and correctly distinguishes subgroup validity from completeness, but it lacks a source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Symmetry-Representative Geometry
children.top_down_role: Canonical ordering, fundamental-domain, and polyhedral structures underlying static and dynamic symmetry handling.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Fundamental Domains for Integer Programs with Symmetries — Friedman
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Fundamental Domains for Integer Programs with Symmetries — Friedman

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Polytopes Associated with Symmetry Handling — Hojny and Pfetsch
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Symmetry-breaking polytopes, symresacks, orbisacks, and orbitopes

children.title: Representative-Selection Orders
children.top_down_role: Ordering families used to organize canonical representatives.

children.title: Lexicographic Orders
children.top_down_role: Lexicographic representative-selection geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is invariant under a finite permutation group \(G\).
Coordinates are equipped with a fixed total order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lex-leader set contains exactly one distinct vector from each \(G\)-orbit in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographically maximal representatives are used; reversing the order gives the equivalent minimal convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a total order of the coordinates of \(x\in X\). The lexicographic representative set for the action of a finite group \(G\) is
\[
 L_G=\{x\in X:x\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}gx\text{ for every }g\in G\}.
\]
Because every finite orbit has a unique lexicographically maximal distinct vector, \(L_G\) intersects each orbit \(Gx=\{gx:g\in G\}\) in exactly one point. Stabilizers may yield several group elements attaining that same representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lexicographic symmetry breaking keeps the unique lexicographically maximal vector from each finite symmetry orbit.
knowledge_statements.title: Lexicographic Orders

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits Lexicographic Orders, and the unique distinct lexicographic representative claim is correct for finite permutation orbits, but no citation is supplied.

children.title: Precedence-First-Use Order Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Representative selection based on activation or first-use conventions.

children.title: Precedence Orders
children.top_down_role: Representative orders based on prescribed priority relations among interchangeable objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Precedence Orders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A basic precedence convention for interchangeable labels with explicit usage indicators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For interchangeable labels \(1,\ldots,k\), let \(z_j=1\) exactly when label \(j\) is used. The precedence order is imposed by
\[
z_1\ge z_2\ge\cdots\ge z_k.
\]
Equivalently, using label \(j\) requires every lower-indexed label \(h<j\) to be used. Hence the active labels are \(\{1,\ldots,q\}\) for some \(q\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\), eliminating solutions that differ only by gaps in the numbering of interchangeable labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A precedence order requires every used label to be preceded by all lower-numbered labels, so active labels form a prefix.
assumptions_latex: Labels \(1,\ldots,k\) are interchangeable.
\(z_j\in\{0,1\}\) indicates whether label \(j\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities \(z_1\ge z_2\ge\cdots\ge z_k\) force used labels to form an initial prefix.

notation.meaning: Indicator that interchangeable label j is used

children.title: First-Use Orders
children.top_down_role: Representative orders based on the earliest activation or occurrence of interchangeable objects.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Use Orders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Items have a fixed order, and labels are ordered by the position of their first occurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the first-use position of label \(j\) by
\[
p_j=\min\{i:x_{ij}=1\},
\]
with \(p_j=\infty\) when label \(j\) is unused. A first-use order requires that, for some \(q\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\),
\[
p_1<p_2<\cdots<p_q<\infty,
\qquad
p_{q+1}=\cdots=p_k=\infty,
\]
where the first chain is empty when \(q=0\). Thus labels are numbered according to the ordered items at which they first appear, selecting a canonical numbering among interchangeable labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-use order numbers interchangeable labels by the earliest ordered item assigned to each label, with unused labels placed last.
assumptions_latex: \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) assigns ordered item \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) to interchangeable label \(j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\).
Each item receives exactly one label.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the \(q\) used labels, requiring \(p_1<p_2<\cdots<p_q<\infty\) and \(p_{q+1}=\cdots=p_k=\infty\) orders labels by their first assigned items.

notation.meaning: Assignment of item i to label j

children.title: Precedence-to-First-Use Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between precedence conventions and first-activation conventions.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in\{0,1\}^{m\times q}\) is an assignment matrix whose columns represent interchangeable labels.
Every used label after label \(1\) has a predecessor label; unused trailing labels are permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{ij}\le \sum_{k<i}x_{k,j-1}\) for all \(i\) and \(j\ge 2\) if and only if \(f_1<f_2<\cdots <f_r\) for the used labels.

notation.meaning: Binary indicator that item i uses label j.
First row using label j, with infinity for an unused label.

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses precedence or first-use symmetry breaking; a specialized source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary assignment formulation for interchangeable labels, with labels introduced consecutively.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in\{0,1\}^{m\times q}\), and define \(f_j:=\min\{i:x_{ij}=1\}\), using \(f_j=+\infty\) when column \(j\) is zero. Suppose the used columns are exactly \(1,\ldots,r\). The precedence inequalities are
\[
x_{ij}\le \sum_{k=1}^{i-1}x_{k,j-1}\qquad (i=1,\ldots,m;\ j=2,\ldots,q).
\]
They hold precisely when the first uses of the used labels satisfy \(f_1<f_2<\cdots<f_r\). Thus the local predecessor requirement and the global first-use ordering select the same binary assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precedence inequalities requiring an earlier occurrence of each predecessor label are equivalent to strictly ordering the first occurrences of all used interchangeable labels.
knowledge_statements.title: Precedence-to-First-Use Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equivalence is mathematically plausible under the stated consecutive-use convention, but no citation supports this specialized precedence/first-use correspondence. A source must also confirm the exact inequality indexing and formulation.

children.title: Aggregate-Profile Order Family
children.top_down_role: Representative selection based on ordered aggregate characteristics.

children.title: Weight Orders
children.top_down_role: Representative selection using ordered weighted aggregate characteristics.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{m\times q}\), and permutations of the \(q\) columns preserve \(X\).

The row weights \(a_1,
\ldots,a_m\) are fixed before optimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A weight-ordered representative satisfies \(W_1(x)\ge W_2(x)\ge\cdots\ge W_q(x)\).
review_flags: The term weight order has model-dependent conventions, and no supplied locator supports this formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate ordering of interchangeable binary columns by fixed row weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed weights \(a\in\mathbb{R}^m\), define the weight of column \(j\) of \(x\in X\) by
\[
W_j(x):=\sum_{i=1}^m a_i x_{ij}.
\]
A feasible matrix is weight ordered when \(W_1(x)\ge W_2(x)\ge\cdots\ge W_q(x)\). If equal aggregate weights are possible, this convention alone need not choose a unique element of a column-permutation orbit; a prescribed secondary order is required for uniqueness. When the weights encode row priority, the aggregate comparison provides a scalar surrogate for ordering complete column profiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weight order arranges interchangeable columns by nonincreasing sums of fixed row weights, with a secondary rule needed when sums tie.
knowledge_statements.title: Weight Orders

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and fits the leaf, but "weight order" is model-dependent and no inspectable source establishes this convention, its orientation, or the stated interpretation as a profile surrogate.

children.title: Load Orders
children.top_down_role: Representative selection using ordered utilization or assignment loads.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m\times q}\), and permutations of its \(q\) columns preserve feasibility.

The load coefficients \(d_1,
\ldots,d_m\) are fixed model data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A load-ordered representative satisfies \(L_1(x)\ge L_2(x)\ge\cdots\ge L_q(x)\).

notation.meaning: Total load assigned to column j.

review_flags: The supplied sources do not identify a canonical load-order definition for symmetric integer models.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering interchangeable resources or bins by their aggregate assigned load.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given load coefficients \(d\in\mathbb{R}^m\), the load of interchangeable column \(j\) at \(x\in X\) is
\[
L_j(x):=\sum_{i=1}^m d_i x_{ij}.
\]
The matrix \(x\) is load ordered when \(L_1(x)\ge L_2(x)\ge\cdots\ge L_q(x)\). This condition selects at least one representative from every column-permutation orbit because the column loads can always be sorted. It generally does not select exactly one representative: columns having equal load may remain permutable unless an additional profile or index tie-breaker is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A load order sorts interchangeable columns by nonincreasing total assigned load; equal-load columns retain symmetry unless another tie-breaker is imposed.
knowledge_statements.title: Load Orders

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The aggregate-load ordering is coherent and the definition content kind fits the leaf, but no cited source establishes this as the intended load-order convention in symmetric integer models.

children.title: Profile Orders
children.top_down_role: Representative selection using ordered multidimensional aggregate profiles.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in X\subseteq\mathcal{A}^{m\times q}\), where \(\mathcal{A}\) is totally ordered.
Permuting the \(q\) columns preserves \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A profile-ordered representative satisfies \(x_{ullet 1}\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}x_{ullet 2}\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}\cdots\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}x_{ullet q}\).

notation.meaning: Complete ordered profile of column j.
Lexicographic order induced by the order on the alphabet.

review_flags: No supplied locator covers lexicographic profile ordering in symmetry handling.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic ordering of complete interchangeable-column profiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in X\), write \(x_{\bullet j}:=(x_{1j},\ldots,x_{mj})\). A matrix is profile ordered when
\[
x_{\bullet 1}\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}x_{\bullet 2}\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}\cdots\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}x_{\bullet q},
\]
where rows are compared in the fixed order \(1,
\ldots,m\). Sorting the column profiles produces such a representative in every column-permutation orbit. The resulting ordered matrix is unique as a matrix: exchanging identical profiles changes no entries, while exchanging distinct profiles violates the prescribed lexicographic order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A profile order lexicographically sorts complete interchangeable columns in a fixed row order, yielding a unique ordered matrix within each column-permutation orbit.
knowledge_statements.title: Profile Orders

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement gives a coherent lexicographic profile order, but no source supports the convention. In addition, conclusion_latex contains the malformed symbols \(x_{ullet 1}\) and \(x_{ullet 2}\), which must be repaired to use \(\bullet\) once a supported formulation is supplied.

children.title: Canonicalization Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representative selection distinguished by handled group and search dependence.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: A Unified Framework for Symmetry Handling — van Doornmalen and Hojny
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: A Unified Framework for Symmetry Handling — van Doornmalen and Hojny

children.title: Global-Group Canonicalization
children.top_down_role: Representative conventions for the complete global action.

assumptions_latex: A finite group \(G\) acts on a feasible set \(X\).
A fixed total order \(\preceq\) is defined on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The global canonical set is \(C_G:=\{x\in X:x\preceq gx\ \forall g\in G\}\), and \(|C_G\cap Gx|=1\) for every orbit when the order distinguishes distinct points.

notation.meaning: Full symmetry group acting on the model.

review_flags: The definition is standard group-action canonicalization, but no supplied locator addresses symmetry representatives.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical representatives under the complete symmetry group of the feasible model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a finite group \(G\) act on \(X\), and fix a total order \(\preceq\) on \(X\). The globally canonical representative of an orbit \(Gx\) is its \(\preceq\)-minimum element. Equivalently, the global canonical set is
\[
C_G:=\{x\in X:x\preceq gx\text{ for every }g\in G\}.
\]
If \(\preceq\) distinguishes distinct points, then every orbit intersects \(C_G\) in exactly one point. Replacing \(X\) by \(C_G\) therefore removes all multiplicity caused by the specified global action without removing any orbit of feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global canonicalization retains the unique order-minimal point of every orbit under the model's full symmetry group.
knowledge_statements.title: Global-Group Canonicalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a mathematically standard definition of global canonicalization and the definition content kind fits the topic, but the record supplies no citation or locator supporting its use in the stated symmetry-optimization context.

children.title: Subgroup Canonicalization
children.top_down_role: Representative conventions restricted to selected subgroups or factors.

assumptions_latex: A finite group \(G\) acts on a feasible set \(X\), and \(H\le G\).
A fixed total order \(\preceq\) is defined on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subgroup canonical set is \(C_H:=\{x\in X:x\preceq hx\ \forall h\in H\}\), selecting one point per \(H\)-orbit but not necessarily per \(G\)-orbit.
review_flags: The definition is standard subgroup canonicalization, but the supplied locators do not support its optimization use.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonicalization restricted to a chosen symmetry subgroup or group factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\le G\) be a selected subgroup. Relative to a total order \(\preceq\), define
\[
C_H:=\{x\in X:x\preceq hx\text{ for every }h\in H\}.
\]
Thus \(C_H\) contains the \(\preceq\)-minimum point of every subgroup orbit \(Hx\). When the order distinguishes distinct points, each \(H\)-orbit has exactly one representative in \(C_H\). Because a full orbit \(Gx\) may decompose into several \(H\)-orbits, subgroup canonicalization can leave symmetry induced by elements of \(G\setminus H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgroup canonicalization keeps one ordered representative per selected-subgroup orbit, while symmetries outside the subgroup may remain.
knowledge_statements.title: Subgroup Canonicalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subgroup-orbit formulation is coherent and correctly distinguishes subgroup from full-group canonicalization, but it has no source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Node-Dependent Canonicalization
children.top_down_role: Representative conventions adapted to residual search-tree symmetry.

assumptions_latex: A finite symmetry group \(G\) acts on the root feasible set \(X\).
A search node \(u\) has local domain \(X_u\subseteq X\).
A total order \(\preceq_u\) is fixed for the residual action at \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The node-canonical set is \(C_u:=\{x\in X_u:x\preceq_u gx\ \forall g\in G_u\}\), where \(G_u:=\{g\in G:gX_u=X_u\}\).

notation.meaning: Feasible domain remaining at search node u.
Setwise stabilizer of the node domain.

review_flags: Residual symmetry may be defined differently by solver frameworks; no supplied locator fixes the intended convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonicalization under the residual group preserving a branch-and-bound node domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At search node \(u\), let \(X_u\subseteq X\) be the domain imposed by the branching history and define its residual symmetry group by
\[
G_u:=\{g\in G:gX_u=X_u\}.
\]
For a total order \(\preceq_u\), the node-dependent canonical set is
\[
C_u:=\{x\in X_u:x\preceq_u gx\text{ for every }g\in G_u\}.
\]
It selects one representative from each \(G_u\)-orbit in \(X_u\). Both the residual group and the representative convention may change with \(u\), but canonicalization must use only transformations preserving the current node domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each search node, canonicalization uses the residual symmetries preserving that node's domain and retains one representative from each residual orbit.
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Dependent Canonicalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The setwise stabilizer construction is mathematically coherent, but residual symmetry at a search node is framework-dependent. A specialized source is required to establish that this is the intended node-dependent canonicalization regime.
