children.title: Cross-Component Residual Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Remaining symmetry that links components treated as independent.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Component Residual Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorwise canonicalization does not remove symmetries that exchange isomorphic components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y=\{(0,0),(0,1),(1,1)\}\) be the internally sorted binary pairs, and set \(X=Y\times Y\). Suppose symmetry restrictions canonicalize each pair separately but omit the component swap \(\tau(a,b)=(b,a)\). Then \(x=((0,0),(0,1))\) and \(\tau x=((0,1),(0,0))\) both satisfy every within-component restriction, are distinct, and belong to the same orbit under the group generated by the internal pair permutations and \(\tau\). Hence complete factorwise handling can still leave cross-component residual symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even when every component is internally canonical, exchanging two isomorphic components can produce a second surviving equivalent solution.
assumptions_latex: \(X=Y\times Y\) with identical component domains.
Within-component restrictions select the sorted pairs in \(Y\).
The component swap \(\tau\) is a model symmetry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both \(x\) and \(\tau x\) survive, so within-component enforcement does not eliminate the cross-component swap.
review_flags: The example is directly verifiable, but no supplied source covers cross-component residual symmetry.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two displayed survivors are related by the component swap, but the internal pair permutations do not act on X=Y×Y because Y already contains only sorted pairs. A source or corrected ambient-space formulation is needed.

children.title: Representation-Obscured Symmetry Boundary
children.top_down_role: Symmetry missed by the selected formulation or detection representation.

children.title: Hidden Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Symmetry not exposed by the selected detection or handling mechanism.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic model symmetry absent from the automorphism group exposed by a chosen representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an optimization model have feasible set \(X\) and objective \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\mathcal R\) be a chosen syntactic representation with detected automorphism group \(A(\mathcal R)\). A hidden symmetry relative to \(\mathcal R\) is a bijection \(g:X\to X\) satisfying \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), while \(g\notin A(\mathcal R)\) under the representation's variable-and-constraint action. Hiddenness is representation-relative: an equivalent reformulation may expose \(g\) as a syntactic automorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hidden symmetry preserves feasibility and objective values but is not visible as an automorphism of the model representation supplied to the detector.
assumptions_latex: \(g:X\to X\) is bijective.
\(\mathcal R\) is a fixed syntactic representation of the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(f\circ g=f\) and \(g\notin A(\mathcal R)\), then \(g\) is hidden relative to \(\mathcal R\).

notation.meaning: automorphism group exposed by the representation
semantic symmetry of the optimization problem

review_flags: The supplied inventory has no locator defining representation-relative hidden symmetry in integer models.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation-relative idea fits the hidden-symmetry leaf, but no source defines it. Membership g∉A(R) requires an explicit identification of syntactic automorphisms with their induced bijections on X.

children.title: Model-Obscured Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Symmetry concealed by the chosen formulation or model encoding.

assumptions_latex: The integer model has feasible set \(F\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) and objective \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\).
An encoding \(E\) presents the model to a detector whose recognized automorphism group is \(H_E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_E\subsetneq G\), so some true model symmetries are invisible in the chosen representation.

notation.meaning: Group of feasible-set bijections preserving the objective.
Symmetries recognized from the encoded representation.
Model encoding supplied to the symmetry detector.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports representation-obscured symmetry; a symmetry-processing source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes mathematical symmetry from symmetry visible in a particular encoded model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=\{g:F\to F: g\text{ is bijective and }f(gx)=f(x)\text{ for every }x\in F\}\). Define the representation-visible subgroup by \[G_E=\{g\in G:\text{there exists }h\in H_E\text{ such that }E(gx)=h(E(x))\text{ for every }x\in F\}.\] Model-obscured symmetry occurs when \(G_E\subsetneq G\). Equivalently, there is a nonidentity \(g\in G\) whose action on solutions cannot be induced by any automorphism recognized in the encoded variables and constraints. Any symmetry handler restricted to \(H_E\) then leaves the equivalence between \(x\) and \(g(x)\) untreated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model obscures symmetry when an objective-preserving permutation of feasible solutions has no corresponding automorphism detectable in the chosen variable-and-constraint representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Model-Obscured Symmetry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the terminal container, but no cited source with an inspectable locator supports this formal notion. The final claim that every handler restricted to H_E necessarily leaves the equivalence untreated also requires qualification or direct support, since a solver could eliminate the pair through mechanisms not induced by H_E.

children.title: Representation-Recovery Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on recovering latent symmetry from an obscuring representation.

assumptions_latex: The original model has symmetry group \(G\) acting on its feasible set \(F\).
A reformulation has feasible set \(F'\), projection \(\pi:F'\to F\), and detectable group \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recovery is exact precisely when every original symmetry has a compatible detectable lift to \(F'\).

notation.meaning: Projection from reformulated to original feasible solutions.
Original and detectable reformulated symmetry groups.

review_flags: No supplied locator establishes this exact lifting criterion for symmetry recovery.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses compatible group lifting as the boundary between recoverable and irrecoverable representation loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The original symmetry is representation-recoverable through \((F',\pi)\) if there exists an injective homomorphism \(L:G\to H\) satisfying \[\pi(L(g)y)=g(\pi(y))\qquad\text{for every }g\in G\text{ and }y\in F'.\] Exact recovery additionally requires that every detectable action relevant after projection arise this way, namely \(H/\ker(\rho)\cong G\), where \(\rho(h)(\pi(y))=\pi(hy)\) is well defined. The recovery boundary is crossed when no such compatible lift exists: then at least one original orbit cannot be reconstructed from detectable reformulation orbits without information absent from the representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetry is recoverable exactly when every original group action has a detectable, projection-compatible lift in the reformulated model.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Recovery Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits a recovery-boundary leaf, but the exact lifting and quotient criterion has no cited support. Moreover, an abstract isomorphism H/ker(rho) congruent to G does not by itself establish that the induced image equals the given action of G; the source must establish the precise action-compatible criterion.

children.title: Inactive Subsymmetry Gap
children.top_down_role: Locally valid symmetry left untreated because activation conditions are not recognized.

assumptions_latex: A branch-and-bound node is identified by an activation state \(\alpha\) and residual feasible set \(F_\alpha\).
The residual objective is \(f_\alpha:F_\alpha\to\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A gap exists when some nontrivial \(G_\alpha\) is valid but is neither recognized nor activated by the solver.

notation.meaning: Residual feasible set under activation state alpha.
Symmetry group of the residual subproblem.
Subgroup actually handled at the state.

review_flags: A dedicated source for activation-dependent subsymmetry detection is missing from the supplied locators.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers conditional symmetries valid only after branching decisions or other local activations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each activation state \(\alpha\), define \[G_\alpha=\{g:F_\alpha\to F_\alpha:g\text{ is bijective and }f_\alpha(gx)=f_\alpha(x)\text{ for every }x\in F_\alpha\}.\] Let \(K_\alpha\leq G_\alpha\) be the subgroup actually handled after the solver recognizes \(\alpha\). An inactive subsymmetry gap occurs if there exists a reachable \(\alpha\) with \(G_\alpha\neq\{e\}\) and \(K_\alpha\subsetneq G_\alpha\) because the activation predicate for the missing subgroup is not recognized. Consequently, distinct members of at least one local orbit remain eligible for separate search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gap occurs when a reachable subproblem has a valid nontrivial symmetry that the solver fails to activate and handle.
knowledge_statements.title: Inactive Subsymmetry Gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind matches the stated role of untreated activation-dependent subsymmetry. No source with a specific locator supports the activation-state formulation, the subgroup K_alpha, or the asserted search consequence.

children.title: Solver-Interaction Failures
children.top_down_role: Adverse interactions between symmetry handling and the surrounding optimization search.

children.title: Symmetry-Processing Break-Even Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where symmetry-processing cost outweighs search reduction.

children.title: Detection Overhead
children.top_down_role: Solver cost incurred while identifying symmetry structures.

assumptions_latex: Symmetry detection is executed once or at specified search nodes.
Runtime is measured in a fixed computational environment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Detection is beneficial only if its downstream search savings exceed \(T_{\mathrm{det}}\) together with all other symmetry-processing costs.

notation.meaning: Total runtime spent constructing and solving symmetry-detection instances.
Detection time at search state s.
Set of states at which detection runs.

review_flags: The supplied sources do not provide a symmetry-detection cost model or complexity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An operational runtime bound, not a worst-case graph-automorphism complexity claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If detection runs at states \(D\), its additive runtime overhead is \[T_{\mathrm{det}}=d_0+\sum_{s\in D}d(s),\] where \(d_0\) includes construction of the root representation and \(d(s)\) includes updating the representation, invoking the detector, and translating returned generators. Thus total symmetry-enabled runtime satisfies \(T_{\mathrm{sym}}\geq T_{\mathrm{det}}\). Relative to baseline runtime \(T_0\), detection alone can break even only if the gross reduction in all other work is at least \(T_{\mathrm{det}}\); otherwise enabling detection cannot reduce total runtime under the stated accounting convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Detection adds its root and node-level computation times; search savings must at least cover this total before symmetry processing can improve runtime.
knowledge_statements.title: Detection Overhead

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this runtime decomposition. The statement is an operational accounting definition and break-even condition, not a complexity bound: it gives neither an input-size-dependent upper or lower bound nor a complexity guarantee. A sourced replacement should use a mathematical role such as definition, property, or condition.

children.title: Handling Overhead
children.top_down_role: Solver cost incurred while enforcing or maintaining symmetry handling.

assumptions_latex: A solver applies symmetry restrictions, propagation, or orbit computations during search.
Each invocation has nonnegative measured computational cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Handling breaks even only when avoided baseline work is at least \(T_{\mathrm{handle}}\), after detection cost is accounted for separately.

notation.meaning: Total cost of enforcing or exploiting already detected symmetry.

review_flags: The supplied locators do not document runtime accounting for symmetry-handling operations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exploitation cost from the cost of initially detecting symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After a symmetry description has been obtained, define handling overhead by \[T_{\mathrm{handle}}=h_{\mathrm{setup}}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_h}h_j,\] where \(h_{\mathrm{setup}}\) covers installation of symmetry constraints or data structures and \(h_j\) covers the \(j\)-th propagation, canonicalization, orbit test, or symmetry-specific update. Since every term is nonnegative, \(T_{\mathrm{sym}}\geq T_{\mathrm{handle}}\). With detection charged separately, symmetry handling can improve total runtime only if the work avoided through its restrictions is at least \(T_{\mathrm{handle}}\); equality is the handling break-even boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Handling overhead is setup plus all enforcement and orbit-processing costs; avoided search work must cover that amount for handling to pay off.
knowledge_statements.title: Handling Overhead

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited source documents this handling-cost decomposition. The selected complexity_bound kind is incorrect because the formula defines measured additive overhead and a break-even condition rather than bounding complexity as a function of problem size. A sourced replacement should use definition, property, or condition.

children.title: Search-Reduction Break-Even Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where symmetry-processing cost does or does not offset reduced search.

assumptions_latex: Baseline and symmetry-enabled runs use the same instance, stopping rule, and computational environment.
Runtime is decomposed into symmetry overhead and non-symmetry search work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Symmetry processing is beneficial, neutral, or harmful according as \(S\) is greater than, equal to, or less than \(O\).

notation.meaning: Gross runtime saved by reducing ordinary search work.

review_flags: This accounting identity is standard, but a symmetry-specific empirical or theoretical source is not supplied.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines runtime break-even under a fixed solver configuration and common stopping criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W_0\) be baseline search work and \(W_{\mathrm{sym}}\) the corresponding non-symmetry work after symmetry processing. Set \(S=W_0-W_{\mathrm{sym}}\) and \(O=T_{\mathrm{det}}+T_{\mathrm{handle}}\). Under additive runtime accounting, \[T_{\mathrm{sym}}-T_0=O-S.\] Hence the beneficial regime is \(S>O\), the break-even boundary is \(S=O\), and the harmful regime is \(S<O\). If node cost is nonuniform, \(S\) must measure saved runtime rather than merely the reduction in node count; fewer explored nodes alone does not establish that the break-even condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetry processing pays off exactly when the runtime saved by reduced search exceeds detection and handling overhead, not merely when node count falls.
knowledge_statements.title: Search-Reduction Break-Even Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind and terminal placement are appropriate, and the algebra is consistent once the additive accounting convention is assumed. However, no symmetry-specific source or explicit standard-field rationale supports the decomposition or its interpretation as a solver-performance boundary.

children.title: Search-Subsystem Interference Family
children.top_down_role: Unfavorable interactions with primal heuristics, branching scores, separation, or tree balance.

children.title: Heuristic Interference
children.top_down_role: Adverse effects of symmetry restrictions on primal heuristics.

assumptions_latex: A primal heuristic \(A\) maps a search state and seed to a set of candidate solutions.
A symmetry handler restricts candidates to a representative region \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Heuristic interference occurs when representative restriction worsens the heuristic outcome under the fixed evaluation budget.

notation.meaning: Candidate set generated by the primal heuristic.
Representative region retained by symmetry handling.
Best objective value found within a candidate set.

review_flags: No supplied source treats interactions between symmetry restrictions and primal heuristics.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational boundary for minimization heuristics under equal budgets and coupled random seeds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, let \(q(C)=\inf\{f(x):x\in C\cap F\}\), with \(q(C)=+\infty\) when \(C\cap F=\varnothing\). Couple baseline and symmetry-enabled executions by the same state information, seed \(\omega\), and evaluation budget. Heuristic interference occurs when \[q(A_{\\mathrm{sym}}(s,\omega)\cap R)>q(A_0(s,\omega)),\] or when the symmetry-enabled heuristic requires greater time to attain the same incumbent value. This can occur even though \(R\) contains an optimal orbit representative, because the heuristic trajectory need not be equivariant and may fail to generate the representative corresponding to a discarded candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetry interferes with a heuristic when, under the same budget and seed, representative restrictions delay or worsen the incumbent it finds.
knowledge_statements.title: Heuristic Interference

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but there is no supporting source. The expression A_{\\mathrm{sym}} contains a malformed doubled backslash before mathrm. The comparison also invokes A_sym and A_0 without defining them in the assumptions or notation, and 'same state information' does not by itself ensure comparable solver states.

children.title: Branching Interference
children.top_down_role: Adverse effects on branching scores, choices, or tree balance.

assumptions_latex: A branching rule assigns scores \(b_s(v)\) to branching candidates at state \(s\).
A symmetry group \(G_s\) acts on the candidates valid at \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Non-invariant scores can make representative choices alter the branching tree and increase search cost despite eliminating symmetric nodes.

notation.meaning: Branching score at search state s.
Symmetry group acting at state s.
Measured cost of the resulting search tree.

review_flags: A source for symmetry-aware branching invariance and adverse tree effects is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers adverse changes in branching decisions, tree shape, or per-node work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Branching is symmetry-compatible at state \(s\) if \[b_s(gv)=b_s(v)\qquad\text{for every }g\in G_s\text{ and valid candidate }v,\] with tie-breaking also constant on orbits. Branching interference is possible when this condition fails and symmetry handling forces or favors a representative \(gv\) different from the baseline choice \(v\). It is realized when, under the same termination rule, the resulting tree \(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sym}}\) has \(C(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sym}})>C(\mathcal{T}_0)\), where \(C\) measures total runtime or weighted node work. A reduced node count does not preclude interference if the retained nodes are more expensive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branching interference arises when branching scores or tie-breaking are not orbit-invariant and symmetry-driven representative choices produce a costlier search tree.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching Interference

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits branching interference, but no source supports the proposed orbit-invariance condition or the causal link from its failure to adverse tree cost. The statement correctly says interference is possible rather than inevitable, yet its formal realization and cost metric still need authoritative support.

children.title: Cut Interference
children.top_down_role: Adverse interactions between symmetry handling and cut separation.

assumptions_latex: At relaxation \(P_s\), a cut generator returns a valid cut family \(C(P_s)\).
A group \(G_s\) preserves the integer subproblem at state \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cut interference is possible when generated cuts are not orbit-closed or symmetry restrictions change cut efficacy enough to worsen search.

notation.meaning: Cut family generated from a relaxation.
Symmetry group of the integer subproblem.

review_flags: The provided cut references do not specifically support symmetry-cut interference.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Addresses compatibility between symmetry handling and dynamically generated cutting planes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cut generator is symmetry-compatible at \(s\) if \[c\in C(P_s),\ g\in G_s\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(c)\in C(P_s),\] where \(g(c)\) is the inequality obtained by applying \(g\) to its variables. Cut interference can occur when this orbit-closure condition fails, or when symmetry constraints change \(P_s\) so that separation selects materially weaker cuts. It is realized if the symmetry-enabled run, under equal separation and termination budgets, has greater total separation-plus-search cost or a weaker bound at the same budget than the baseline, despite retaining validity of every generated cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut interference occurs when cut generation is not orbit-compatible or symmetry restrictions induce weaker separation and a worse bound or runtime under equal budgets.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut Interference

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the cut-interference leaf, but the claim lacks a symmetry-specific source. The action g(c) is not fully defined for general inequalities, and preservation of the integer subproblem alone does not ensure that the same group acts compatibly on the relaxation P_s or the generator's cut family.

children.title: Cross-Subsystem Interference
children.top_down_role: Combined performance effects spanning multiple solver subsystems.

assumptions_latex: A solver uses at least two interacting subsystems under a fixed stopping rule.
Each subsystem can be enabled with or without symmetry processing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero interaction term shows that subsystem effects are not additive; a positive term is adverse cross-subsystem interference.

notation.meaning: Runtime with symmetry settings indicated by binary indices.

review_flags: A symmetry-specific source for factorial subsystem-interaction analysis is not supplied.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines interference by a controlled two-subsystem difference-in-differences comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two symmetry-sensitive subsystems, let \(T_{ij}\) be runtime when their symmetry-related modifications have settings \(i,j\in\{0,1\}\), all other settings being fixed. Define \[I=T_{11}-T_{10}-T_{01}+T_{00}.\] Cross-subsystem independence corresponds to \(I=0\). Cross-subsystem interference is present when \(I\neq0\); for a minimization-of-runtime evaluation, \(I>0\) is adverse because the joint setting costs more than the sum of its isolated effects predicts. The same definition applies to another loss metric, provided all four runs use the same instance, budget, stopping rule, and sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-subsystem interference is the nonadditive performance effect measured by a controlled difference-in-differences comparison of two symmetry-sensitive solver components.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Subsystem Interference

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The difference-in-differences formula is internally coherent under fixed experimental controls, but no source establishes it as the intended notion of symmetry-related cross-subsystem interference. The record primarily introduces an operational definition or performance measure, so condition is a weak content-kind fit unless a source explicitly presents a zero-interaction condition.

children.title: Reformulation-Induced Symmetry Effects
children.top_down_role: Symmetry altered or recreated by presolve, decomposition, lifting, and auxiliary variables.

children.title: Transformation Effects
children.top_down_role: Changes to visible or valid symmetry caused by model transformations.

assumptions_latex: A transformation \(T:F\to F'\) maps feasible solutions and preserves objective values through \(f'=f\circ T^{-1}\) when invertible.
The original symmetry group is \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bijective transformations preserve abstract symmetry by conjugation; nonbijective or representation-sensitive transformations may lose, merge, or introduce detectable symmetries.

notation.meaning: Conjugate symmetry group after a bijective transformation.

review_flags: The model-transformation locator is only indirectly relevant; symmetry-specific full text is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates preservation of abstract solution symmetry from changes in detectable formulation symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T:F\to F'\) is bijective and objective preserving, then every \(g\in G\) induces \(g'=T\circ g\circ T^{-1}\), and \[G'=TGT^{-1}\cong G.\] Thus a bijective transformation preserves the abstract orbit structure, although \(G'\) may be harder or easier to detect syntactically. If \(T\) is not bijective, this conclusion need not hold: identified solutions can merge original orbits, omitted coordinates can conceal actions, and added representational degrees of freedom can create symmetries absent from the original variables. Therefore formulation-level symmetry is not invariant under arbitrary model transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bijective objective-preserving transformations conjugate the symmetry group, while nonbijective transformations can conceal, merge, or create formulation-level symmetries.
knowledge_statements.title: Transformation Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits transformation effects, and the conjugation statement for a bijective objective-preserving transformation is mathematically standard. However, no source is cited, and the broader claims about nonbijective transformations concealing, merging, or creating formulation-level symmetries require a symmetry-specific locator or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Effects
children.top_down_role: Symmetry created, obscured, or altered by auxiliary variables.

assumptions_latex: An extended formulation has feasible set \(Q\subseteq X\times Y\) and projection \(P=\pi_X(Q)\).
A group \(H\) acts on \(Q\) and preserves its extended objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Auxiliary variables create fiber symmetries in \(\ker\rho\) and preserve a base symmetry only when that symmetry admits a compatible lift.

notation.meaning: Symmetry group of the extended formulation.
Induced action homomorphism on original variables.

review_flags: No supplied source directly addresses symmetry groups of extended formulations with auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes projected, liftable, and purely auxiliary symmetries of an extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h\in H\), suppose \(\pi_X(h(x,y))\) depends only on \(x\). Then \(h\) induces \(\rho(h):P\to P\) by \(\rho(h)(x)=\pi_X(h(x,y))\), and \(\rho:H\to\operatorname{Sym}(P)\) is a homomorphism. Elements of \(\ker\rho\) move only auxiliary realizations and are fiber symmetries invisible in the original variables. An original-variable symmetry \(g\) survives the extension exactly when \(g\in\operatorname{im}\rho\), equivalently when some \(h\in H\) satisfies \(\pi_X(h(x,y))=g(x)\) for every \((x,y)\in Q\). Hence auxiliary variables may add fiber symmetry while preventing some base symmetries from lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary variables can add symmetries within projection fibers, while an original symmetry survives only if it lifts compatibly to the extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits auxiliary-variable effects, but no source supports the lifting characterization. To make rho a homomorphism into Sym(P), the induced maps must be well defined on fibers and bijective on P; the statement explicitly assumes only the first point. The phrase 'survives the extension exactly when' also depends on whether H is the full extended symmetry group or merely a selected detectable subgroup.

children.title: Presolve-Induced Symmetry Changes
children.top_down_role: Symmetry changes arising specifically from presolve reformulation.

assumptions_latex: The original integer model is \(M=(F,f)\), with feasible set \(F\subseteq D\) and objective \(f:F\to\mathbb R\).
Presolve produces a reduced model \(M'=(F',f')\) together with a solution-lifting map \(L:F'\to F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only reduced-model symmetries that lift to objective-preserving symmetries of the original model support exact symmetry handling.

notation.meaning: objective-preserving symmetry group of model M

review_flags: No supplied locator directly addresses the interaction between presolve and symmetry groups.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-symmetry boundary for reduced models equipped with a solution-lifting map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{Sym}(M)=\{g:gF=F,\ f(gx)=f(x)\text{ for all }x\in F\}\). A reduced-model permutation \(h\in\operatorname{Sym}(M')\) represents an original symmetry only if there exists \(g\in\operatorname{Sym}(M)\) such that \(L(hy)=g(Ly)\) for every \(y\in F'\). Presolve may remove visible generators by fixing, aggregating, or eliminating variables, and it may create interchangeability in the reduced representation. Exact orbit pruning based on \(h\) is transferable to \(M\) only under this lifting condition; otherwise the apparent reduced symmetry is not an exact certificate for the original model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Presolve can hide or create visible interchangeability. A reduced symmetry is safe for exact orbit pruning only when lifting commutes with an objective-preserving symmetry of the original model.
knowledge_statements.title: Presolve-Induced Symmetry Changes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and local topic fit, but no source supports the presolve–symmetry lifting claim. The stated lifting map alone does not specify objective correspondence, coverage of original solutions, or the conditions under which reduced-model pruning preserves the original problem.

children.title: Decomposition-Induced Symmetry Changes
children.top_down_role: Symmetry changes arising when a model is divided into coordinated subproblems.

assumptions_latex: The variable index set has a decomposition \(I=I_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_k\), where \(I_0\) denotes master variables.
The original model has exact symmetry group \(G\) acting on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The symmetry usable inside the fixed decomposition is the subgroup of \(G\) preserving its block structure, unless the full decomposition algorithm is equivariant under block permutations.

notation.meaning: exact symmetry group of the undecomposed model
partition into master and subproblem variable blocks
setwise stabilizer of the block partition

review_flags: The source supports decomposition structure; the symmetry-stabilizer formulation requires direct symmetry literature review.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-block and block-permuting symmetries in decomposition algorithms.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed decomposition \(\mathcal P\), transformations usable independently within its subproblems belong to \(G_{\mathcal P}=\{g\in G:g(I_0)=I_0,\ \{g(I_1),\ldots,g(I_k)\}=\{I_1,\ldots,I_k\}\}\). A transformation mixing variables across blocks without mapping whole blocks to whole blocks is not a symmetry of the decomposed representation. Even when \(g\in G_{\mathcal P}\) permutes subproblems, exact symmetry handling additionally requires the master variables, generated cuts or columns, subproblem states, and selection rules to transform equivariantly. Otherwise decomposition reduces the usable group to the subgroup stabilizing all maintained algorithmic structures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decomposition retains only symmetries compatible with its blocks and algorithmic state. Block permutations remain usable only when master data, subproblems, generated objects, and selection rules transform equivariantly.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Induced Symmetry Changes

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited decomposition chapter supports decomposition structure, not the asserted symmetry stabilizer or algorithmic equivariance conditions. The record also alternates between a block-permuting stabilizer and a subgroup usable independently within fixed subproblems; the required subgroup depends on the algorithm and needs direct support.

children.title: Dynamic-State Loss
children.top_down_role: Loss of search-dependent symmetry information after restarts, copying, or tree rewrites.

assumptions_latex: At search state \(S\\), the solver uses a subgroup \(G_S\) that preserves the current node domain and all active symmetry data.
A restart, copy, or tree rewrite maps the state to \(R(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Search-dependent symmetry information remains valid after the state transformation only when it is transported equivariantly and revalidated for \(R(S)\).

notation.meaning: symmetry subgroup valid at state S

review_flags: No supplied locator covers stateful symmetry handling across restarts or tree rewrites.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and completeness boundary for search-dependent symmetry state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dynamic information such as orbit representatives, stabilizer chains, handled-orbit markers, and node-local symmetry restrictions is valid only relative to its search state \(S\). After transformation to \(R(S)\), retained data must be transported by a state map \(T_R\) satisfying equivariance with the surviving group action and must be revalidated against the domain and constraints at \(R(S)\). Discarding such data can forfeit symmetry reductions but does not invalidate an otherwise complete search. Reusing stale data without equivariant transport can incorrectly identify distinct subproblems or suppress unexplored representatives, so exact pruning must stop until valid symmetry state is reconstructed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restarts, copies, and tree rewrites may erase useful symmetry state. Lost data weakens pruning; stale data is unsafe unless transported equivariantly and revalidated at the new search state.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-State Loss

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and statement match Dynamic-State Loss, but no source establishes the claimed lifecycle and safety conditions for stateful symmetry data. The first assumption also contains malformed TeX, `\(S\\)`, which must be repaired when a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.title: Symmetry-Validity Boundary Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Boundaries separating exact, valid symmetry handling from heuristic analogy or material owned by other chapters.

children.title: Invalid Apparent Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Apparent interchangeability invalidated by objectives, constraints, domains, data, or semantics.

assumptions_latex: The optimization model is \(\min\{f(x):x\in F\}\), with \(F\subseteq D\).
A proposed variable transformation \(g:D\to D\) is bijective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transformation is an exact model symmetry precisely when it preserves both feasibility and objective values; otherwise treating its classes as orbits is invalid.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly states the exact symmetry criterion for integer models.
standard_field_rationale: exact model symmetry requires preservation of domains, feasibility, and objective values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validity test for a proposed model automorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The transformation \(g\) is an exact symmetry of the optimization model if and only if \(g(F)=F\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). Thus visual similarity or repeated coefficients is insufficient whenever \(g\) changes a variable domain, violates a constraint, alters fixed data or boundary conditions, changes an objective coefficient, or interchanges objects with distinct application semantics. If either feasibility preservation or objective preservation fails, the equivalence classes generated by \(g\) are not valid solution orbits, and deleting all but one representative can remove a feasible or optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apparent interchangeability is exact only when it preserves domains, every constraint, and objective values. Any violation makes orbit-based deletion or pruning mathematically invalid.
knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Apparent Symmetry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasibility-and-objective criterion is standard, but no inspectable source is supplied. The record additionally treats distinct application semantics as invalidating a mathematical model symmetry without defining semantic preservation or including semantics in the model, so the intended notion of symmetry must be clarified and sourced.

children.title: Approximate-Symmetry Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary between exact orbit reduction and heuristic treatment of near-symmetry.

assumptions_latex: The model is \(\min\{f(x):x\in F\}\), and \(g\) is a bijection of the ambient domain.
Nonnegative tolerances \(\varepsilon_F\) and \(\varepsilon_f\) quantify feasibility and objective discrepancies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact orbit reduction applies only at zero discrepancy; positive-tolerance near-symmetry requires a separate error-certified method or heuristic treatment.
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses approximate symmetry or error-certified near-symmetry reduction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between exact orbit pruning and tolerance-dependent near-symmetry handling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\delta_F(g)=0\) mean \(g(F)=F\), and let \(\delta_f(g)=\sup_{x\in F}|f(gx)-f(x)|\) whenever \(g(F)=F\). Exact orbit reduction is justified only when \(\delta_F(g)=\delta_f(g)=0\). Conditions such as \(\delta_F(g)\leq\varepsilon_F\) and \(\delta_f(g)\leq\varepsilon_f\) with a positive tolerance define near-symmetry, not an equivalence preserving the optimization problem. Consequently, representative deletion or symmetry-based pruning is heuristic unless an independent bound proves that the permitted discrepancy cannot alter feasibility, the required optimality tolerance, or the incumbent comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero feasibility and objective discrepancy permits exact orbit reduction. Positive discrepancy defines near-symmetry and is heuristic unless an independent error bound protects feasibility and the desired optimality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Symmetry Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits the approximate-symmetry failure boundary, but `\delta_F` is defined only through its zero case and is then used in a numerical tolerance inequality. A genuine feasibility-discrepancy metric, its domain, and the claimed error guarantees require authoritative support.

children.title: Application-Model Ownership Boundary
children.top_down_role: Application-specific formulations remain in their model chapters, with this chapter retaining symmetry structures and handling interfaces.

assumptions_latex: An application formulation is represented by \(M=(D,F,f,\Sigma)\), including its domain, constraints, objective, and application semantics.
A group \(G\) is proposed to act on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The application chapter owns the formulation and semantics; the symmetry chapter owns the action, validity conditions, orbit structures, and symmetry-handling interface.

notation.meaning: proposed symmetry group acting on the model domain

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: separates application-model specification from reusable symmetry theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Knowledge-ownership interface between application formulations and reusable symmetry theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an application model \(M=(D,F,f,\Sigma)\), the application-specific chapter specifies \(D\), derives \(F\) and \(f\), and records the semantics \(\Sigma\) that determine which objects may be interchanged. The symmetry chapter receives the interface \((M,G)\) and determines whether \(g(F)=F\), \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\), and whether \(g\) respects \(\Sigma\) for all \(g\in G\). It owns group actions, orbits, stabilizers, symmetry detection, and exact handling conditions, but does not replace the derivation or interpretation of the underlying application formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Application chapters define and justify their models and semantics. The symmetry chapter studies proposed group actions, validates them, and supplies reusable orbit, detection, and handling concepts.
knowledge_statements.title: Application-Model Ownership Boundary

children.title: General Integer-Optimization Ownership Boundary
children.top_down_role: General formulations, cutting planes, branching, decomposition, and complexity remain in their dedicated chapters.

assumptions_latex: A general integer-optimization method \(\mathcal A\) solves models \(M\) without requiring symmetry.
A symmetry module \(\mathcal S_G\) augments \(\mathcal A\) using an exact model-symmetry group \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: General algorithmic theory remains owned by its dedicated topic; the symmetry chapter owns only the group-dependent augmentation and its correctness interface with that theory.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinguishes general optimization machinery from symmetry-specific augmentations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Knowledge-ownership interface between general integer optimization and symmetry-specific augmentations.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The formulation of integer programs and the general theory of valid inequalities, cutting planes, branching, decomposition, relaxations, and complexity belong to their respective integer-optimization topics and are represented by a base method \(\mathcal A\). The symmetry chapter studies an augmentation \(\mathcal S_G(\mathcal A)\) only through structures depending on an exact group \(G\): orbit reduction, symmetry-aware branching or propagation, canonical representatives, and compatibility with solver state. Correctness of \(\mathcal S_G(\mathcal A)\) must preserve the feasibility and optimality guarantees of \(\mathcal A\); it does not redefine the underlying general method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General formulations and algorithms stay in their dedicated chapters. The symmetry chapter covers only group-dependent augmentations and the conditions under which they preserve the base method's guarantees.
knowledge_statements.title: General Integer-Optimization Ownership Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal Value over a Feasible-Set Division
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-value decomposition for a finite covering of the feasible set; disjointness is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $z_{\mathrm{IP}}=\max\{cx:x\in S\}$ and $z_{\mathrm{IP}}^i=\max\{cx:x\in S^i\}$ for $i=1,\ldots,k$. If $\bigcup_{i=1}^kS^i=S$, then $z_{\mathrm{IP}}=\max_{i=1,\ldots,k}z_{\mathrm{IP}}^i$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If finitely many subsets cover the feasible set, the optimal value over the full set equals the largest optimal value among the corresponding subproblems. The subsets may overlap.
assumptions_latex: \bigcup_{i=1}^kS^i=S
z_{\mathrm{IP}}=\max\{cx:x\in S\}
z_{\mathrm{IP}}^i=\max\{cx:x\in S^i\}\quad(i=1,\ldots,k)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z_{\mathrm{IP}}=\max_{1\le i\le k}z_{\mathrm{IP}}^i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A maximization algorithm using nested outer feasible-set relaxations and successively tighter objective overestimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $t=1$, $w^*=+\infty$, and $z^*=-\infty$. Choose $S\subseteq S_R^1$ and $z_R^1(x)\ge cx$ for every $x\in S$. At iteration $t$, solve $z_R^t=\max\{z_R^t(x):x\in S_R^t\}$ and let $x^t$ be an optimizer. If $x^t\in S$ and $z_R^t=cx^t$, set $w^*=cx^t=z^*$ and terminate with $x^t$ optimal. Otherwise, when $x^t\in S$, set $w^*=z_R^t$ and $z^*=cx^t$; then refine so that $S\subseteq S_R^{t+1}\subseteq S_R^t$ and $cx\le z_R^{t+1}(x)\le z_R^t(x)$ for all $x\in S$, with at least one of the feasible-set or objective relaxations changed, and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with an outer relaxation of the feasible set and an objective function that upper-bounds the true objective on the feasible set. Solve the relaxation. If its optimizer is feasible and its relaxed value equals its true value, it is optimal. Otherwise record the relaxation value and, when available, the feasible value, then strictly refine either the relaxed set or the objective overestimator while retaining validity.
assumptions_latex: \max\{cx:x\in S\}\text{ is the target integer program}
S\subseteq S_R^1
z_R^1(x)\ge cx\quad\forall x\in S
S\subseteq S_R^{t+1}\subseteq S_R^t
cx\le z_R^{t+1}(x)\le z_R^t(x)\quad\forall x\in S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^t\in S\ \land\ z_R^t=cx^t\ \Longrightarrow\ x^t\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in S}cx
